title: Step 1 integration tests: long-running task simulation (wait-or-defer + single-flight)
description: Integration tests (NO mocks; real test workflow) simulating a workflow with a deliberately LONG-running command. Build a test workflow/command whose _process_command sleeps longer than wait_seconds (configurable) to deterministically simulate the ~10-min LLM call. Assert: (1) a turn exceeding wait_seconds returns a deferred response (running + turn_key) WITHOUT orphaning the execution; (2) a retry with the same args returns the SAME turn_key and starts NO second execution (assert the long command body runs exactly once, e.g. via a call counter/log); (3) the execution still completes and persists after the request returned; (4) §3.3: a retry arriving before /initialize startup completes receives exec_state=running + startup_turn_key, never an empty startup_output; (5) the fast path returns the result inline when the command is quick; (6) no ctx mutation outside runtime.lock; (7) process_message DeprecationWarning no longer emitted. Follow tests/ conventions (integration only).
notes:
TEST SCOPE NARROWING (per user): Test ONLY /initialize with a startup_action so NO workflow training is required (no trained intent models needed — a startup_action dispatches a command directly by name, bypassing NLU/intent detection). Build/extend a small test workflow with a command whose _process_command sleeps for a configurable duration to simulate the long-running LLM call. Drive everything through POST /initialize (startup_action -> submit_turn(kind='initialize_startup')). Concretely assert: (1) FAST PATH — when the startup command is quick (sleep < wait_seconds), /initialize returns 200 inline with startup_output + exec_state=DONE; (2) DEFER — when sleep > wait_seconds, /initialize returns 202 with startup_turn_key + exec_state=running WITHOUT orphaning the execution; (3) SINGLE-FLIGHT RETRY (§3.3) — a second /initialize for the same channel arriving before startup completes hits the 'already exists' branch and returns the SAME startup_turn_key + exec_state=running (NEVER an empty startup_output), and the sleeping command body runs EXACTLY ONCE (assert via a call counter / log); (4) the deferred execution still completes and persists after the request returned; (5) the process_message DeprecationWarning is no longer emitted. Skip the /invoke_agent and /invoke_assistant agent-path assertions here (those require trained models) — cover them separately if/when training fixtures exist.
WORKFLOW TEMPLATE (per user): The hello_world example is a good template for the small test workflow. See tests/hello_world_workflow/ (and fastworkflow/examples/hello_world/) — a minimal application/ + _commands/ pair (e.g. add_two_numbers.py with a Signature.Input/Output + ResponseGenerator). Clone that structure into a new fixture (e.g. tests/long_running_workflow/) and make the command's _process_command sleep for a configurable duration (read from the Input params or an env var) to simulate the long LLM call. Because the test drives it via /initialize startup_action (direct dispatch by command name), no plain_utterances/generate_utterances/training is needed — the Signature can be minimal. Reuse the existing tests/ conftest fixtures and conventions.
close_reason: tests/test_fastapi_turns_async.py: fast-path inline, defer+single-flight (one execution across retries), pointer-based 409. Driven via /initialize startup_action against tests/hello_world_workflow (no training). Full suite 457 passed.

title: /api/turns re-parses every span's attributes across the whole store per request (6 s at 165 turns; 49-59 s under 4 concurrent)
description:
Measured 2026-09-29 on the working tree of feat/experiment-observability-3.3 against the owner's real store ~/.local/state/fastworkflow/workflows/ido_workflow/observability.sqlite3 (615 MB: 165 turns, 50,807 spans, 505 MB of span attribute JSON), through an in-process ChatbotServer opened read-only.

- GET /api/turns (rail default): 6.12 s, 1.15 MB. With facets=false: 4.26 s. Turn-finder page (limit=50&scan_limit=500): 2.98 s.
- 4 concurrent GET /api/turns: 49.4 / 54.6 / 56.2 / 59.4 s -- worse than running them serially (~24 s): CPU-bound work on ThreadingHTTPServer threads contends on the GIL.
- cProfile of search_turns + annotate_turn_rows (7.5 s): 133,012 json.loads for ~50k spans. diagnosis.search_turns -> turn_markers runs over ALL 165 turns, not the page (2.35 s); annotate_turn_rows -> turn_span_stamps (3.6 s) where cost_rollup/usage_rollup, count_llm_calls_cut_at_limit and turn_decision_signals each re-decode the same span attributes (server._mapping_attr, comparison.attributes); store.spans_for_turns fetchall pulls whole attribute blobs (1.3 s).

Cost grows with every recorded span, and nothing is cached although a finished turn's spans never change. By contrast /api/turn/<key> for the largest trace (634 spans) is 0.19 s, and /api/navigation is 0.05 s.

Fix direction: (1) decode each span's attributes once per request and hand decoded spans to every stamp helper; (2) select only the attribute keys the stamps and markers need (json_extract) instead of whole blobs; (3) persist or cache per-turn stamps/markers keyed by (turn_key, span count/last span id); (4) single-flight identical in-flight queries. diagnosis.py and store.py are shared with the agent-facing reads, so keep semantics.
design:
Design review (2026-09-29, before implementation). Options:
A. Decode once + reuse page spans: search_turns already decodes each span in turn_markers; annotate_turn_rows then re-fetches the page's spans and re-decodes them ~3x (cost_rollup/usage_rollup, cut-at-limit, decision signals). Reuse the decoded spans for page rows. Cost low, risk low. Saves ~3.6 s of the 6.1 s.
B. In-process derived cache keyed by (store identity, turn_key, span count, max span rowid, query params that affect markers: low_confidence_below, loop_policy). Finished turns are immutable; the key check is one cheap GROUP BY over idx_spans_trace, so appended spans invalidate automatically. Bounded LRU. Opt-in parameter to search_turns so agent-facing callers keep today's behaviour unless they pass it. Cost medium, risk low-medium (staleness guarded by the key).
C. Serialize heavy scans (one semaphore): 4 concurrent requests degrade to 49-59 s each from GIL contention; queuing makes them ~serial. Cost low, risk low.
D. json_extract only needed keys in SQL: rejected, helpers spread across modules read many keys; high semantic risk.
E. Persist markers at write time: rejected, schema change under the fresh-schema rule; high cost/risk.
Chosen: A + B + C. Acceptance relaxed for cold start (cold cost is dominated by reading 505 MB of attribute JSON, which only D/E remove): cold <= 50% of today (<= 3 s), warm < 300 ms, 4 concurrent warm requests each < 1.5 s, byte-identical payloads vs. current for a golden query set.
acceptance_criteria: On the same store: /api/turns < 1.5 s cold and < 500 ms warm; 4 concurrent requests each < 2 s; payload byte-identical to current output for a golden set of queries (markers, facets, low-confidence, scoped).
notes: Triage (2026-09-29): priority=P1; cost=medium; risk=medium. P1: the rail/turn finder is the debug mode's main entry and is already multi-second on a modest real store, degrading superlinearly. Medium cost (decode-once is local; caching needs invalidation design); medium risk because diagnosis semantics are shared with agent reads.
close_reason: Derived-turn LRU cache (64 MB budget, keyed on store identity/turn/span count+max rowid/status/policy), scan semaphore, decode-once, batched span fetch. ido store: cold 6.1s->2.6s, warm ~17ms, 4 concurrent 49-59s->24-76ms, peak RSS 1.2GB->~400MB; golden /api/turns output byte-identical. Verified with targeted test files only; full suite not run (user instruction, 2026-09-29).

title: Enforce framework-owned user approval for commands annotated approval-mandatory or approval-delegatable
description:
Framework-enforced user approval for commands the workflow declares as needing it. Redesigned 2026-09-28 per owner guidance; supersedes the read/write design of 2026-09-27 (kept in the notes as history). Priority P1 | Cost high | Risk high. DEFERRED. Not built.

## Owner guidance (2026-09-28)

- Do not gate by read vs write. Some writes are easy to undo and are as harmless as read-only commands.
- Exactly two approval annotations exist: `approval-mandatory` and `approval-delegatable`. Anything not annotated, the agent executes at its own discretion (no gate).
- `approval-delegatable`: the user may delegate the decision. The implementation looks for evidence of delegation in user-specific config, and, while no delegation is in place, learns the user's decision patterns/heuristics.
- `approval-mandatory`: non-undoable actions (e.g. sending a critical email). Approval is always required.

## Annotation

- Per command in the runtime manifest (`workflow_runtime.json`, `runtime_manifest.CommandDeclaration`): new optional field `approval: "mandatory" | "delegatable"`. Absent = agent discretion.
- Independent of the existing `effect` contract (read_only/write/unknown), which stays for observability (`tracing.consequence_assessment`) and the fix-hfbr finish-check gate.
- `CommandDeclaration` is a strict model (unknown fields rejected), so an older engine will refuse a manifest carrying `approval`. Gate it as a manifest feature (e.g. `approval_policy` v1) or bump `schema_version`; document the forward-compatibility break.
- Core/CME commands carry no annotation (never gated).

## Where it is enforced (unchanged from the 2026-09-27 analysis)

- Origin stamp: a contextvar set at `_execute_workflow_query` entry (covers the agent and the intent-clarification sub-agent). Do not use `workflow.context["is_user_command"]`.
- Gate: `CommandExecutor._invoke_command_impl`, after the qualified command name and validated parameters are final and before the response generator runs; backstop check in `perform_action`. Only agent-originated calls are gated; direct user paths (assistant mode, `/` commands, `/perform_action`, MCP tool calls) are the user's own instruction.
- Lookup failure or no manifest = no annotation = no gate (consistent with "unannotated = discretion").

## approval-mandatory

- Never satisfied by delegation config, learned heuristics, or operator settings.
- Pending approval stored as PRIVATE session state (WorkflowExecutionContext, beside `_awaiting_user`), never in `workflow.context` or the ReAct stash; bound tuple = {one-time id, qualified name, `input_obj.model_dump(mode="json")`, target context identity, turn key, channel}; serialized with the session (additive key, or ride a SCHEMA_VERSION bump); FastAPI must persist while an approval is pending.
- Framework-rendered prompt from the bound tuple (never agent text), e.g. "The agent wants to run send_email to X with {...}. This cannot be undone. Reply yes to approve or no to decline."
- Reply intercepted at `_resume_agent_message` / `_ask_user_tool` before the planner rewrite; deterministic parse, only exact normalized "yes" approves; the framework executes the STORED tuple exactly once; anything else declines. Single use; cleared at turn end, `/cancel_pending`, new turn.
- Unattended (no user can answer): refuse immediately ("approval required; no user available").

## approval-delegatable

Resolution order at the gate:
1. **Delegation config.** Look up a user-specific delegation store for a rule covering this call. If one matches, execute without prompting and record `approval: delegated` with the rule id.
   - Rules are scoped: qualified command name, optional parameter constraints (equality, allow-lists, numeric limits), optional context type, optional expiry and use count.
   - The store is keyed by user identity (FastAPI: the JWT `uid` claim; CLI: the OS user or a configured id) and lives outside anything the agent can write, e.g. `<state_root>/users/<user_id>/delegations.json` or a table in the user's store. It is edited only through a user- or operator-authenticated path (a CLI command / an authenticated API endpoint), never through agent tools.
   - No user identity (anonymous) = no delegation = behave as mandatory.
2. **Otherwise prompt exactly as for mandatory**, and record the decision in a per-user decision log: {qualified command, context type, parameter features (redacted / hashed values plus shape), decision, timestamp, turn/session ids}. The log is also outside the agent's reach.
3. **Learning (while no delegation is in place).** From the decision log, derive the user's decision patterns per (command, parameter pattern): approval rate with counts and recency.
   - Use them to (a) show the user a hint in the prompt ("you approved this 9 of 9 times"), and (b) propose a delegation rule once a pattern is stable (e.g. n >= k decisions, 100% approve, no recent denial), which the user accepts or rejects; accepted proposals become delegation-config rules.
   - Learned patterns never auto-approve by themselves, and there is no "adopt learned rules automatically" opt-in (owner decision 2026-09-28).
   - When a pattern reaches the proposal threshold, the framework prompts the user to explicitly approve or decline delegating that specific rule (framework-rendered text naming the command, the parameter constraints and scope; answered on the user channel with the same anti-forgery rules as an approval: exact "yes" only, never agent text). Approved -> written to the delegation config as a user-approved rule (recorded with the pattern id and the approval time). Declined -> remembered, and not proposed again until the pattern changes materially or a cooldown passes.
   - Proposal prompts are never shown unattended; they wait for the next interactive turn.

## Unattended runs

- Mandatory: refused. Delegatable: delegation config applies (this is how sanctioned automation runs); without a matching rule, refused. Unannotated: runs.
- Simulated-user harnesses (ido run_simulated_operator, tau2-style) answer the framework prompt as the user; strict yes/no still applies. Scripted experiment runner must stop / mark failed when a turn ends awaiting approval rather than blindly sending its next message.
- Replaces the 2026-09-27 shadow/enforce/deny modes plus deferred "operator pre-approval": keep a `shadow` mode for rollout (record what would have been gated), and `enforce`; operator pre-approval is subsumed by delegation config.

## Why the agent cannot approve for the user

- It cannot create or modify pending approvals, delegation config, or the decision log (no agent tool reaches them).
- Its own `ask_user("reply yes")` is an ordinary clarification, not an approval.
- Agent-written text (thoughts, planner rewrite, summaries, `raw_user_message`) never counts as approval.
- Parameters/target cannot drift after approval: the framework executes the stored tuple.
- Learned patterns cannot approve without explicit user delegation.

## Interaction with fix-hfbr

fix-hfbr's finish check now names only steps whose commands are declared `read_only`. Once this gate exists, the safe set for the note becomes "not approval-annotated, or annotated and gated": unannotated commands are at agent discretion by definition, and annotated ones end in the framework gate. Revisit the fix-hfbr gate then (it could use the approval annotation instead of the effect contract).

## Known limits

- The framework guarantees the approver is not the in-process agent and saw a framework-rendered prompt; it cannot prove a human is on the user channel (simulators, MCP clients, scripted drivers). MCP has no elicitation support here.
- Annotations are trusted, not enforced: an unannotated command that is actually non-undoable, or a command calling another command's ResponseGenerator directly (ido command_compose), is not gated.
- One prompt per call; batch approval is future work.

## Suggested staging

1. Annotation + gate + mandatory flow (+ shadow mode), with the execute-once / no-retry fix (`execute_workflow_query` retries on Exception).
2. Delegatable with delegation config and the per-user decision log.
3. Learning: pattern stats, prompt hints, delegation proposals (and the optional opt-in, if the owner wants it).

## Tests (integration, no mocks)

A test workflow with a real `workflow_runtime.json` declaring one mandatory, one delegatable and one unannotated command, driven through real suspend/resume in both topologies: unannotated runs without prompt; mandatory prompts with framework text and executes the stored params once on "yes" only (not "sure", "/yes", or agent text); delegatable runs without prompt when a matching rule exists and prompts otherwise; decisions land in the log; a stable pattern produces a proposal but no auto-approval; anonymous user = mandatory behaviour; unattended refuses mandatory and unmatched delegatable; cross-process resume keeps the pending approval; `/cancel_pending` clears it.
notes:
2026-09-28: deferred by owner (high cost or high risk triage).
HISTORY (superseded 2026-09-28 by owner guidance: approval-mandatory / approval-delegatable annotations instead of read/write gating). Original 2026-09-27 description follows verbatim:

Framework-enforced user approval before the agent executes a `write` command, in a way the agent can never satisfy on the user's behalf. Design agreed with the owner on 2026-09-27, in the follow-up to the adversarial review of 01b0d64 / 43e42a2. Priority P1 | Cost medium | Risk high (risk = impact of leaving it unfixed: today confirmation before writes is prompt-only; ido's own notes record writes licensed by "proceed using your own judgement"). Not built yet.

This supersedes the "treat writes specially in the finish-check note" options for fix-hfbr. Once this gate exists the note can safely name any unexecuted step, including write steps, because any attempt to run one ends in a framework prompt to the user. fix-hfbr then reduces to rewording the note and fixing needs_user parsing (whole step text, wider approval phrasing).

## Principle

Approval is a framework-owned state transition, not something said in the conversation. The agent may REQUEST a write; only the framework EXECUTES it, and only after a genuine inbound user-channel message answers a prompt the framework itself rendered.

## Scope decision (owner, 2026-09-27)

Only commands whose runtime-manifest effect is `write` are gated. Undeclared commands (`unknown`) are treated the same as `read_only` FOR NOW. Consequences: workflows without a manifest (all three test workflows, embedded contexts, the CME workflow) are unaffected; the guarantee covers declared writes only. Revisit once manifests are common.

## Mechanism

1. Origin stamp. A contextvar set at `_execute_workflow_query` entry (workflow_agent.py ~181; also covers the intent-clarification sub-agent at ~171/178). Do NOT reuse `workflow.context["is_user_command"]` (workflow_agent.py:626, `iteration_counter <= 0`): it is true for the agent's first call each turn, after ask_user, and after forced replans.
2. Gate. In `CommandExecutor._invoke_command_impl`, after `command_name` / `cmd_parameters` are final (command_executor.py:307-308) and before `response_generation_object(...)` (:333-340). Same check in `perform_action` (:409, :463) as a backstop, though the agent cannot reach it today. Effect looked up on the canonical qualified name (e.g. `Resource/add_tag`), via `get_runtime_metadata` / `load_manifest`; lookup failure = unknown = not gated (per scope decision).
3. Pending approval. For an agent-originated `write`, do not run it. Store {one-time id, qualified name, `input_obj.model_dump(mode="json")`, target context identity (`command_context_for_response_generation` + instance_label), turn key, channel id, rendered prompt} as a PRIVATE attribute of WorkflowExecutionContext (next to `_awaiting_user` / `_pending_clarification_request`, ~159-161), not in workflow.context / cme context (commands and NLU write those) and not in the ReAct stash (LLM output). Serialize it in `serialize_state` (~949-984) / `apply_serialized_state`; bump session_state_store SCHEMA_VERSION 4 -> 5; FastAPI must persist while an approval is pending (today it saves only if `awaiting_user or has_open_command()`, utils.py ~1005-1016).
4. Suspend with framework text. Raise the existing AskUserSuspend path so ReAct stashes the trajectory (react.py:391-413). The question is rendered by the framework from the stored record, never by the agent, e.g. "The agent wants to run apply_remediation on Account 'Alan' with {...}. Reply yes to approve or no to decline." If `_turn_outputs` shows the same (name, params, target) already succeeded this turn, say so in the prompt.
5. Intercept the reply before the agent sees it. At `_resume_agent_message` (workflow_execution_context.py ~2002-2022, Topology B) and `_ask_user_tool` (workflow_agent.py ~560, Topology A), before `_post_ask_user_response` / the planner rewrite (`build_query_with_next_steps`, ~843). Deterministic parse, no model: only an exact normalized "yes" approves.
   - yes: the framework executes the STORED bound tuple exactly once (never re-routes agent text), records the output, and the agent's observation is "User approved; result: ...".
   - anything else: nothing runs; the agent sees "User declined" plus the raw reply as an ordinary user message.
   - The record is single-use and is cleared at turn end, on `/cancel_pending` (`cancel_pending` / `_reset_agent_suspension`, ~1166-1180, 1798-1806), and on a new turn.
   - A `/`-prefixed reply during suspension is routed deterministically today and does not resume the agent (~1391-1402); it must count as "not approved".
6. Agent guidance. Tell the agent (tool description) that the framework confirms writes itself, so it should not ask its own confirmation question first (avoids double prompts).

## Why the agent cannot approve for the user

- It cannot create or modify the pending record (no agent tool reaches WEC private state).
- Its own `ask_user("reply yes to continue")` is an ordinary clarification, not an approval; a subsequent write attempt still gets the framework's prompt.
- Agent-written text never counts as approval: thoughts, planner rewrite of the reply, conversation summaries in `_refine_user_query` (~2335-2348), `raw_user_message`.
- Parameters/target cannot drift after approval: the framework runs the stored tuple.
- Repeats are prompted again, with "already ran this turn" when applicable.

## Modes (deployment setting; reuse the runtime-manifest feature `side_effect_safety` v1, declared at runtime_manifest.py:166 with modes off/shadow/enforce but currently read by nothing)

- `shadow`: log/record what would have been gated; nothing blocked. Roll out here first to measure how often ido's writes trigger a prompt.
- `enforce` (target default everywhere, including unattended runs): prompt as above. Fails safe with nobody present: the prompt is never answered, so the write never runs; the turn ends awaiting approval.
- `deny`: refuse agent writes immediately without prompting; the agent sees "write refused: no user available to approve this" and can finish its answer. For batch/scripted/CI/startup runs.
- Operator pre-approval: DEFERRED until a real sanctioned-automation use exists. If built: explicit allow-list of qualified command names (never "all writes"), deployment config only (unreadable/unwritable by the agent), every allowed execution recorded as `operator_preapproved`.

## Unattended runs (owner-agreed recommendation)

- Simulated-user runs (ido harness run_simulated_operator.py / constant_operator.py, tau2-style): keep `enforce`. The simulator is the user by design and answering the framework prompt is the realistic test; strict yes/no means "proceed using your own judgement" no longer approves. Costs: trajectories change, so re-run ido baselines before comparing; simulator instructions may need to say it can answer yes or no.
- No-one-present runs: `enforce` is safe; `deny` is cleaner. The scripted experiment runner (experiment/runner.py ~1150-1154) sends its next scripted message without checking status, so under `enforce` a scripted "yes" would approve: use `deny` there, and fix the runner to stop / mark the attempt failed when a turn ends awaiting approval.
- Existing test suite unaffected (no test workflow declares a write); new tests set the mode explicitly.

## Known limits (accepted, document them)

- The framework guarantees the approver is not the in-process agent and saw a framework-rendered prompt; it cannot guarantee a human is on the user channel (simulators, MCP clients, scripted drivers). MCP has no elicitation support here (fastapi-mcp 0.4.0 owns call_tool; mcp_specific.py:32-35).
- The manifest is trusted, not enforced: a command declared read_only that writes, or a command that calls another command's ResponseGenerator directly (ido application/command_compose.py), is not gated.
- Direct user paths (assistant mode, `/` commands, `/perform_action`, MCP tool calls, FastAPI `/invoke_assistant`) are treated as the user's own instruction and are not gated; external callers there may be LLMs (possible later option to gate them).
- One prompt per write; batch approval is future work.
- Standing permission ("do it without asking") earlier in the turn is not honoured in v1.
- Undeclared (`unknown`) commands are not gated (scope decision above).

## Related fixes to include

- `execute_workflow_query` retries the whole command on Exception (workflow_agent.py ~632-643), which can re-run a write whose post-processing raised: do not retry after a gated write executed.
- Scripted experiment runner status check (above).

## Tests (integration, no mocks)

A small test workflow with a real `workflow_runtime.json` declaring one `write` command and one `read_only` command, driven through the real suspend/resume paths in both topologies:
- agent write -> framework prompt text (not agent text) -> "yes" executes the stored params once; "no", "sure, go ahead", "/yes" and any other reply do not execute;
- agent cannot approve via its own ask_user; changing params after approval runs nothing new without a new prompt;
- cross-process resume with a pending approval (serialize/restore, schema v5);
- `/cancel_pending` and a new turn clear the pending approval;
- `shadow` records but does not block; `deny` refuses without prompting;
- read_only and undeclared commands are never gated;
- repeat of an already-executed write says so in the prompt.

2026-09-28 owner decision: learned delegation rules are never adopted automatically; when a pattern hits the threshold the user is prompted to explicitly approve or decline delegating that rule. Description updated.

title: Stop the finish-check note from driving duplicate side effects or bypassing confirmation gates
description:
Found in adversarial review of 01b0d64 (fix-ufot follow-up) and 43e42a2 (fix-4dsr). Priority P1 | Cost medium | Risk high (risk = impact of leaving it unfixed). Not fixed yet.
Review item: E01. Commits: 43e42a2. Concerns: features, reliability. Related: fix-4dsr (43e42a2, finish-time plan check).

Evidence: finish_check.py:406-408 NOTE_TAIL "Run them if they are still needed…"; measured precision 0.77 (~1 in 4 flags is a step that did run); turn_plan.py:115-117 is_checked only excludes optional/needs_user; text-plan fallback sets needs_user=bool(_APPROVAL_RE.search(lead)) on the first 40 chars only (turn_plan.py:138-143,185). title: Offload evidence sidecar is created world-readable (0644 in a 0755 dir) when observability is off
description: Security. RuntimeHandleArchive creates <observability.sqlite3>.offload-handles.sqlite3 without chmod, and state_paths.workflow_state_dir uses os.makedirs with the default mode. When the observability store runs, it hardens the parent dir to 0700 and its own DB to 0600 (store.py:1589, 1692 [R4]), which hides the problem. With FW_OBSERVABILITY off -- the DEFAULT for library embedders -- the store never runs, and the sidecar holding raw command responses (customer emails, addresses, payment ids) lands 0644 in a 0755 dir. Reproduced 2026-09-24: 'workflow state dir: 0o755, sidecar file: 0o644'. This is exactly the failure design review R4 (docs/fastworkflow_observability_studio_design_review.md:72-88) was written to prevent. Fix now, independent of the consolidation: create the sidecar (and its -wal/-shm) 0600 and its parent dir 0700 in the archive's own open path, mirroring the store. Superseded by fix-wys2 once the evidence lives in the always-hardened observability DB, but the live default is exposed until then. Test: integration test with FW_OBSERVABILITY=0 asserting file 0600 and dir 0700.
close_reason: Superseded by fix-wys2: the redesign ships in PR #84 itself, so no interim fix; its permission requirement is now an acceptance criterion on fix-wys2.

title: Known-name guard refuses a context's own mixed-case command
description: In intent_detection.py (PR 84), command_name_dict keys keep original case while the typed token and command_inventory() are lowercased. For a command like ListPermissions owned by the current context: exact match misses, foreign_owner_contexts() returns the current context itself, and the turn ends with a false routing hint ('is a command of the Child context, which this context and its parents do not provide'). Before PR 84 the miss fell through to fuzzy/classifier, which usually recovered, so this is a regression for workflows with mixed-case command names. Reproduced at logic level: exact match hits False, foreign owners ['Child']. Bundled examples use lowercase names only. Fix: compare lowercase on both sides (lowercase command_name_dict keys or the lookup), and exclude the current context from the owner list. Add an integration test with a mixed-case command.
close_reason: Fixed: exact match looks the token up case-insensitively and resolves to the key as spelled; foreign_owner_contexts compares lowercase on both sides and drops the current context. title: Selection bootstrap missed two ordinary upgrade paths into the wrong first winner
description:
Two independent gaps in fastworkflow/benchmark/setup.py let a brand-new experiment become the winner of a lineage that already had older recorded runs. Both reproduced with real stores and both fixed in the selection_ui wave; filed so the change is reviewable rather than invisible.

GAP 1 — history in the workflow DEFAULT store, named by no registration. A workflow upgraded from a version that predates selection has its experiments in the one database state_paths.observability_db names for it, and no .experiments/*.json registration names that path. ensure_selection_bootstrap only admitted stores that registrations named plus already-authorized sources, so the contest started empty and the first experiment registered after the upgrade won. The existing test that looked like it covered this calls setup.authorize_evidence_store by hand first, which is the adoption ceremony the design says there is not.
REPRODUCTION: write exp-preexisting into state_paths.observability_db(workflow) with initialize_winner=False and no registration, then setup.create_experiment(...). Before: the new registration is the group winner. After: exp-preexisting is.
FIX: _admit_default_store admits that ONE canonical path, asked for by name (no filesystem discovery), opened read-only, never created, and reports it as a gap that blocks election when it exists but cannot be read.

GAP 2 — a registration store replaced by a DIFFERENT database. _authorize_recorded_store detected the identity mismatch and returned None, which stopped that one bootstrap call from electing, but recorded nothing: a runner starting later opened the control, saw a contest whose visible history looked complete and elected its own new experiment over runs nobody could read.
REPRODUCTION: bind an experiment to a store, swap a different real store in at that path, discard the control, ensure_selection_bootstrap (correctly incomplete), then have an ExperimentController create a newcomer with the same benchmark pin. Before: the newcomer is winner and list_sources holds only the runner store. After: winner is None and the expected old identity is in the contest.
FIX: route the mismatch through _declare_unreadable so the gap lives IN the control where the existing unresolved-source guard already refuses to elect; the impostor identity is never authorized. _source_resolver now identity-checks what it opens and returns None on a mismatch, so the impostor cannot answer for the id and the real file returning to that path recovers automatically.

AFFECTED CODE: fastworkflow/benchmark/setup.py — _source_resolver, _authorize_recorded_store, new _admit_default_store, _seed_registrations(already_missing=), ensure_selection_bootstrap.

TESTS: tests/test_experiment_registration_and_repeat.py — TestTheDefaultStoreIsPartOfTheHistory (4 tests: default-store history holds the contest, a runner reaches the same answer, a workflow that recorded nothing gets no database created, an unreadable default store elects nobody) and TestAStoreReplacedByADifferentOne (3 tests: a later runner still refuses to elect, the impostor never answers for the id it is not, the original coming back recovers by itself). 172 passed across test_experiment_registration_and_repeat / test_benchmark_setup / test_experiment_winner_selection / test_experiment_setup; 276 passed across the selection, chatbot, sealing and workspace suites.

ACCEPTANCE: the seven tests above pass, no existing setup or selection test needs a manual authorize/adopt call added, and source bytes of existing evidence are never written by bootstrap.

title: Select and retain the best run for a task within an experiment
description:
Support multiple-run optimization/distillation using the existing task/attempt screen. After running the same task/setup n times within an experiment, a human or coding agent can select Use as best run for a recorded, finished attempt of that task. This selection is a preferred example, not proof of correctness and not the experiment winner. Before selection, the first completed attempt may be used as a viewing reference explicitly labeled Reference, never automatically Best. Allow leaving the task undecided, clearing a selection, and replacing it. No required score, rubric, numeric target or rationale.
Persist task-scoped selected attempt reference, actor/provenance, timestamp, previous/new references and optional reason; retain history. Reuse winner selection machinery with explicit distinct scope where feasible; support stale-update detection and immutable evidence via existing mutable control metadata/sidecars. Keep every attempt and its actual status visible. Multi-turn attempts include their full conversation, not only the final answer. Task header shows Best run and a Compare other runs action that pins this reference in the shared comparison view. Choosing a best run never changes code, deploys a change, changes experiment winner, or reruns anything.
Teacher/student roles and self-distillation remain independent origins of execution evidence. This task introduces no teacher/student execution engine, extraction pipeline, separate Distillations tab or insight-review system. Chat streaming and final-answer artifacts retain highest delivery priority; reproducibility remains deferred.
acceptance_criteria: After a task has three attempts, either client can select, replace or clear the best run and inspect selection history. Only recorded finished attempts of that task can be selected; actual failed status stays visible if chosen as the preferred example. A provisional viewing reference is never mislabeled Best. Real-store and browser interaction tests cover this without paid runs.

Task-best writes selection_pointers/selection_decisions with scope_kind=task_best and scope_key = <experiment_id>\x1ftask\x1f<task_id>, through a new generic primitive SelectionControlStore.apply_scoped_decision / scoped_pointer / scoped_history. WHAT MAY BE CHOSEN. Only a recorded attempt of THIS task with execution_finished_at set (the [XR13] execution completion marker). title: F5b - Add ResultHandleStore.open_readonly via an overridable _connect seam, plus the historical-store acceptance bracket
description:
F5b of the framework task split - the contract-INDEPENDENT half of Revision 4's F5, split
per the independent review of the design, which judged F5 overloaded for one task on the
critical path. Design:
/home/drawal/rl/devreview-artifacts-20260919/adapter-boundary-report-rev4.md section 5.

*** THIS TASK IS STARTABLE TODAY. It has no dependency on the adapter contract, on F1-F4,
or on either accepted condition. It is the framework-side counterpart of IDO's I1. ***

WHY IT EXISTS, MEASURED. Revision 3 claimed that additive `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`
under new names is what keeps a historical store safe, with read-only opens as a secondary
measure. Revision 4 section 5.2 measured that this is BACKWARDS, on copies in /tmp with
the source file verified byte-identical before and after:

  Probe A - construct today's ResultHandleStore over a copy of a real frozen artifact:
            sha256 CHANGES; five tables added.
  Probe B - emit only the post-F5a `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS result_handle_batches`:
            sha256 CHANGES; +8192 bytes.
  Probe C - the same CREATE over a `mode=ro` URI: REFUSED with
            "attempt to write a readonly database"; sha256 unchanged.

An additive CREATE describes the SCHEMA delta, not the FILE delta - it is itself a
byte-level mutation. The read-only open is the mechanism that actually holds.

THE HAZARD IS LIVE TODAY, BEFORE ANY RENAME. Merely constructing a ResultHandleStore over
a frozen artifact rewrites it. Verified against the working tree at 1c6992e:
ResultHandleStore.__init__ is store.py:44-167 and runs five CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS
(store.py:52, :80, :112, :135, :147) plus two CREATE INDEX (store.py:96, :160) over a
read-write connection; `_connect` is store.py:169-172 with no URI, no mode=ro and no flag.
There is no read-only constructor: a search of store.py and paging.py for mode=ro,
immutable, readonly, read_only, open_readonly and uri=True returns no matches outside
prose comments. F5a does not create this hazard; it adds a sixth table to it. That reframes
this task from "part of a schema migration" into "the moment a live footgun gets fixed",
which is why it is split out and why it can start now.

OWNER'S RESOLUTION OF REVISION 4's OPEN QUESTION (section 9.3, "which side owns the -shm
sidecar policy"). Revision 4 listed three options and declined to choose, inclining toward
option 2 (a framework `immutable` parameter). THE OWNER HAS RULED, AND IT IS NONE OF THE
THREE. Read-only store opens use an OVERRIDABLE `_connect` SEAM mirroring
ReadOnlyObservabilityStore, with IDO subclassing it - the pattern IDO already uses at
evaluation/observability.py:204-227. NO NEW FRAMEWORK PARAMETER.

The framework-side precedent is real and re-verified at 1c6992e:
fastworkflow/observability/store.py:5463-5504 is ReadOnlyObservabilityStore. Its __init__
(:5472-5494) never runs the create/migrate block, and its `_connect` override
(:5496-5504) connects through `file:{db_path}?mode=ro` with uri=True. Its docstring
(:5464-5470) states the rule this task copies: "Never creates, migrates, or writes the
file... inspecting a DB must not mutate it." ResultHandleStore.open_readonly should be the
same shape, roughly fifteen lines: skip the CREATE TABLE block entirely, connect through
`file:<path>?mode=ro`, and leave `_connect` (store.py:169-172) as the seam a subclass can
override.

RATIONALE WORTH KEEPING, because it is why the judgment does not belong in the framework.
A plain `mode=ro` connection to a WAL-mode SQLite database STILL CREATES an `-shm`
sidecar - that is how 17 sidecars once appeared under the frozen EXP-028 v4 evidence root,
a real incident, not a precaution. `immutable=1` suppresses the sidecar but makes SQLite
ignore the WAL, so on a store with an uncheckpointed WAL it silently reads a TRUNCATED
database. Somebody therefore has to decide, per file, whether immutable=1 is safe, and
that decision needs to know which paths are frozen evidence and which are live run
directories. The framework cannot and should not know that. So the mechanism lives in the
framework and the per-file safe/unsafe judgment lives with the caller that knows the paths.
The same argument already applies to the framework's own observability reader, which
"also serves the live chatbot debug layer, where immutable=1 would be wrong."

HISTORICAL STORES ARE PRESERVED. Revision 4 section 5.1 counts them on the IDO side: 2787
*.sqlite3* files, of which 2729 are published evaluation collections, 47 are frozen
artifacts and 11 are live-ish workflow state; 438 have "handles" in the name and are the
ones a result-handle reader would plausibly be pointed at. Everything in that census is
preserved. Nothing is classified disposable and nothing is deleted. New code must never
open an old-shape file for writing.

THE ACCEPTANCE BRACKET this task owns - steps 1, 3, 4, 6 and the step-7 gate of Revision 4
section 5.4, in order. Steps 2 and 5 assert F5a's schema and are owned there.

  1. Checksum manifest, BEFORE ANYTHING. sha256 and byte size of all 438 *handles*.sqlite3*
     files plus the 47 evaluation/artifacts/** stores, recorded to a manifest OUTSIDE both
     trees.
  3. Read-only-open test, on a COPY of a real historical store. Assert that open_readonly
     over the copy reads what it should, creates no table, creates no -shm or -wal sidecar,
     and leaves the copy's sha256 unchanged. This is probe C promoted to a regression test.
  4. NEGATIVE test. Assert that the WRITING constructor over that same copy DOES change it,
     so that if someone later makes open_readonly silently fall back to read-write, step 3
     fails loudly instead of passing vacuously. This is the step that stops step 3 rotting.
  6. Re-verify the manifest: every checksum from step 1 unchanged.
  7. ONLY THEN may any real workflow state be opened for mutation - which is why this task
     blocks F5a.

Steps 1 and 6 bracket the whole of F5 (both halves), not just this task's own tests. No
step opens anything under a frozen evidence path for writing at any point; every test that
needs a realistic store works on a copy in a temporary directory.
acceptance_criteria:
1. ResultHandleStore.open_readonly exists, skips the CREATE TABLE block entirely, and
connects through file:<path>?mode=ro; `_connect` remains an overridable seam a subclass can
route through its own policy. NO new framework parameter is added - not `immutable`, not
anything else.
2. The shape mirrors fastworkflow/observability/store.py:5463-5504
(ReadOnlyObservabilityStore) closely enough that the precedent is obvious to a reader, and
the docstring records the owner's ruling and the -shm / immutable=1 rationale.
3. Step 1 manifest exists outside both trees, covering the 438 *handles*.sqlite3* files and
the 47 frozen artifact stores, with sha256 and byte size.
4. Step 3 regression test passes on a COPY of a real historical store: reads correctly,
creates no table, creates no -shm or -wal sidecar, sha256 unchanged.
5. Step 4 negative test passes: the writing constructor over the same copy DOES change it.
6. Step 6 re-verification passes: every checksum from step 1 unchanged.
7. No file under a frozen or historical evidence path is opened for writing at any point,
and nothing is deleted.
8. F5a does not start its schema work until steps 1, 3, 4 and 6 have passed.
notes: Container: this task is one of F1-F8 of the framework split held by fix-iq53.2.1. It is filed as a sibling of that container rather than a child because bd treats a parent-child edge to a non-epic parent as a blocker, which would make every F-task permanently invisible to bd ready. The container relationship is expressed as dependency edges from fix-iq53.2.1 onto F1-F8 instead, so fix-iq53.2.1 cannot be closed or shipped before its constituent work lands.

ResultHandleStore.open_readonly + ReadOnlyResultHandleStore: 87 insertions, 0 deletions in store.py, purely additive, mirroring ReadOnlyObservabilityStore with the _connect seam and NO new framework parameter per owner ruling. Acceptance bracket is tests/test_historical_store_acceptance.py, 739 lines, 12 tests, bracketing all 451 historical stores with a non-overwriting checksum manifest, a read-only-open test on a copy, a negative test so step 3 cannot rot into a vacuous pass, and manifest re-verification. Steps 2 and 5 belong to F5a by design. Measured and now regression-tested: the pre-existing hazard (writing constructor over a frozen artifact grows it 135168 -> 192512 bytes with a changed digest and five new tables), that plain mode=ro on WAL DOES create sidecars, and that immutable=1 silently returns 10 rows instead of 2010 against an uncheckpointed WAL. description:
F6 of the framework task split in Revision 4 section 8 of the adapter-boundary design
(/home/drawal/rl/devreview-artifacts-20260919/adapter-boundary-report-rev4.md). OFF the
critical path.

WHAT IT DOES. Prove the contract is not a database abstraction, by exercising it over a
bundled workflow that has no SQL, no offsets, no view and no timeslot - and by showing the
non-paginated half needs no adapter at all.

THE NON-DATABASE EXAMPLE (Revision 4 section 6.6). tests/todo_list_workflow.
TodoListManager.list_todo_lists() and TodoList.get_all_children() return in-memory objects
with stable integer ids and a description. The adapter uses ONE-ITEM LOOKAHEAD: ask for
limit + 1, return limit, and let the extra item answer has-more exactly.

    def todo_source(request):                   # batch callback
        state = request.descriptor["state"]     # opaque to the framework
        after = (request.continuation or {}).get("after_id")
        window = todo_manager.children_after(state["list_id"], after,
                                             limit=request.limit + 1)   # ONE operation
        batch, has_more = window[:request.limit], len(window) > request.limit
        reply = {"rows": [{"id": t.id, "description": t.description} for t in batch]}
        if has_more:
            reply["continuation"] = {"after_id": batch[-1].id}
        return reply                            # claims nothing; that is the terminal's job

    def todo_terminal(request):                 # terminal callback, fired once
        # Lookahead already proved exhaustion, so this costs ZERO backend operations.
        return {"complete": True}

The zero-operation terminal is the point of the example under Revision 4, not decoration.
IDO's terminal performs one backend operation; this one performs zero; the framework's
callback count is identical in both cases. A per-callback allowance could not express that
difference, which is the concrete argument for the separate terminal hook.

CASES TO COVER (Revision 4 section 6.6):
  - Empty, 0 rows / limit 3: one batch callback, zero rows, one terminal callback,
    complete, no continuation.
  - Exact multiple, 6 / 3: exactly two batch callbacks, NO THIRD, one terminal callback
    claiming complete. (Revision 1's `exhausted = len(items) < limit` was wrong and stays
    retracted - on an exact multiple the last full batch is indistinguishable from a
    non-final one. Lookahead is what makes the no-third-call case legitimate here, where
    an offset resolver must still probe.)
  - Partial last, 7 / 3: three batch callbacks, the third returns 1 row, one terminal.
  - No claim offered: the terminal omits `complete`; the page shows source_complete=false,
    incomplete_reason=completeness_not_claimed, continuation=source-incomplete, no cursor.
  - One operation per callback: a counting wrapper asserts at most one backend operation
    per callback and exactly one terminal callback per walk terminal.

THE NON-PAGINATED EXEMPLAR, unchanged and needing no new machinery. A small complete result
declares a ResultHandleSpec with source=None and takes the local path - re-verified at
1c6992e, paging.py:1987 is `plan = "backend-walk" if descriptor else "local"`. Assert no
resolver registered, no source call, source_complete taken from the producer's own
declaration, and that stored rows still page and filter.

DEPENDENCY NOTE. Revision 4 states no dependencies for F6. The F4 edge is INFERRED: the
zero-operation terminal callback and the completeness_not_claimed page cannot be exercised
until the terminal hook exists.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A todo_list_workflow adapter exists using one-item lookahead, with a terminal callback
that performs zero backend operations.
2. All five cases in the description pass as tests, including the exact-multiple case
making exactly two batch callbacks and no third.
3. A counting wrapper asserts at most one backend operation per callback and exactly one
terminal callback per walk terminal.
4. The source=None non-paginated path is exercised: no resolver registered, no source call,
source_complete from the producer's declaration, stored rows still page and filter.
5. No SQL, view, ordering, offset or timeslot concept appears anywhere in the example.
notes: Container: this task is one of F1-F8 of the framework split held by fix-iq53.2.1. It is filed as a sibling of that container rather than a child because bd treats a parent-child edge to a non-epic parent as a blocker, which would make every F-task permanently invisible to bd ready. The container relationship is expressed as dependency edges from fix-iq53.2.1 onto F1-F8 instead, so fix-iq53.2.1 cannot be closed or shipped before its constituent work lands.
close_reason: F6 landed in 0d574c3 (+544). tests/test_result_handles_non_database.py walks the real bundled tests/todo_list_workflow through the same fetch_page a portal-backed handle uses, proving the contract is not a database abstraction. Uses one-item lookahead, never len(rows)<limit -- the three population shapes are pinned at 0 items (one callback, complete-zero), 6 items (EXACTLY two callbacks, no third, which is the case the retracted rule would have needed an extra empty round trip for) and 7 items (three, last carrying one row). test_the_terminal_callback_costs_zero_backend_operations pins operations_per_call == [1,1,1,0]: the terminal spends nothing where IDO's spends a countOnly. NonPaginatedHandleTests is the source=None exemplar. 13 passed exit 0.

title: F7 - Promote the Revision 4 trace harness to permanent callback-budget regression tests
description:
F7 of the framework task split in Revision 4 section 8 of the adapter-boundary design
(/home/drawal/rl/devreview-artifacts-20260919/adapter-boundary-report-rev4.md). OFF the
critical path. This is the framework half of the honest split in section 3.4: the framework
ENFORCES when and how often it calls, and tests - not framework checks - pin what that
discipline actually is.

WHAT IT DOES. Promote the Revision 4 trace harness to permanent regression tests, so a
work-profile regression fails a test rather than showing up as a slow portal months later.

THE HARNESS EXISTS AND IS AT RISK. /tmp/audit-adapter/ currently holds trace_baseline.py,
trace_edges.py, trace_maxima.py, simulate_proposed.py and probe_store_mutation.py with
their raw output traces.json, edges.json, maxima.json, sim.json and probe.json. /tmp IS NOT
DURABLE. Copy it into the repository before it is lost; the independent review verified all
nine trace rows against that raw output and would have no way to re-verify them otherwise.
The harness wraps the existing FakePortal fixture - re-verified at 1c6992e,
tests/test_result_handles.py:987 - in a counting proxy that splits count_only calls from
batch calls and records sequence position.

ASSERTIONS TO PIN (Revision 4 sections 2.1, 2.3, 2.4 and 3.4):
  - At most 9 callbacks per fetch: 8 charged (MAX_RESOLVER_CALLS_PER_FETCH = 8, re-verified
    at paging.py:184) plus at most one uncharged terminal.
  - At most one terminal callback per fetch, and it is ALWAYS THE LAST callback of that
    fetch.
  - A capped walk makes ZERO terminal callbacks - the terminal is reached only by
    exhausting the population, never by exhausting a budget.
  - The unsettled-terminal retry costs ONE callback and ZERO batch reads per later fetch.
  - A cold resume of a settled walk costs ZERO callbacks and still serves every row.
  - The four required shapes with their measured counts: normal (540 rows / page_size 40 /
    3 KB budget -> 6 fetches, 15 callbacks, 14 batch reads, 1 countOnly); filtered (120
    rows all matching -> 6 fetches, 7 callbacks, 6 batch reads, 1 countOnly); exhausted
    (80 rows / 40, an exact multiple so the empty terminal probe is unavoidable -> BBBC);
    capped by call limit (540 rows / page_size 1 -> BBBBBBBB, no countOnly) and capped by
    byte budget (-> BBB, no countOnly).
  - The per-fetch maximum boundary: 280 rows / 40 gives BBBBBBBBC = 9 callbacks and
    source_complete=true; 320 rows / 40 gives BBBBBBBB = 8 and resolver_call_limit; 240
    rows / 40 gives BBBBBBBC = 8 and source_complete=true.

TWO FIXTURE GAPS THE INDEPENDENT REVIEW NAMED, worth closing here. No fixture covers a
portal that errors mid-walk on a BATCH - FakePortal's `fail_at` parameter exists
(tests/test_result_handles.py:998, :1001, :1029) and is used by a test at :1173 but not by
the harness - and none covers a store_unavailable walk. Both are stop-reason paths that the
walk_can_continue allowlist at paging.py:2106-2115 depends on, so they are exactly the
paths where an untested regression would be invisible.

WHAT THESE TESTS DO NOT ESTABLISH, and must not be described as establishing. They measure
WORK - operation counts and placement - not LATENCY, and they are fixture-driven, so they
say nothing about a real portal's behaviour or the relative cost of a count versus a batch
read. The workflow-side half of the invariant (one backend operation per callback inside
the adapter) is I6's counting wrapper, not this task's.

DEPENDENCY NOTE. Revision 4 states no dependencies for F7. The F4 edge is INFERRED: the
terminal-callback assertions cannot run before the terminal callback exists. The harness
capture itself does not need F4 and could be done sooner.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The trace harness and its raw output are committed inside the repository, not left in
/tmp.
2. Every assertion listed in the description is a passing test against the post-F4 code,
with the same shape names Revision 4 section 2.1 uses.
3. The two named fixture gaps are closed: a batch-level mid-walk error using FakePortal's
`fail_at`, and a store_unavailable walk, both asserted against the walk_can_continue
allowlist behaviour.
4. The tests fail if a terminal callback is charged against the purse, if a second terminal
fires in one fetch, if a terminal is not last, or if a capped walk fires one.
5. The test module states in a comment that it measures work and not latency, and that the
workflow-side one-operation-per-callback invariant is I6's.
notes: Container: this task is one of F1-F8 of the framework split held by fix-iq53.2.1. It is filed as a sibling of that container rather than a child because bd treats a parent-child edge to a non-epic parent as a blocker, which would make every F-task permanently invisible to bd ready. The container relationship is expressed as dependency edges from fix-iq53.2.1 onto F1-F8 instead, so fix-iq53.2.1 cannot be closed or shipped before its constituent work lands.
close_reason: F7 landed in d3ba6af (+963). THE HEADLINE EVIDENCE: measured against the IMPLEMENTED contract, all nine walk shapes, all three per-fetch maxima and all four edge cases reproduce Rev 4's PRE-implementation baseline exactly -- same fetches, callbacks, batch reads, sequences and terminal placement. normal 6 fetches/15 callbacks/14 reads/1 terminal; filtered 6/7/6/1; exhausted 1/4/3/1; capped 1/8/8/ZERO terminals. So the terminal callback demonstrably preserved _reconcile's work profile rather than merely promising to, which is what root's Revision 3 review demanded before accepting equivalent latency. Harness moved OUT of /tmp into tests/callback_trace.py (550 lines, still runs standalone), with an untouched backup kept. tests/test_result_handle_callback_budget.py asserts <=9 callbacks/fetch, <=1 terminal/fetch, terminal always last, zero terminals on a capped walk, and the one-callback/zero-batch retry. One real post-F4 behaviour difference is now tested rather than left to be found: a portal answering complete:false is a DECISION, so it settles and later fetches cost nothing, where old _reconcile retried forever. 18 passed / 50 subtests exit 0.

title: F2 - Split SourceRequest into a four-field batch request and a separate TerminalRequest
description:
F2 of the framework task split in Revision 4 section 8 of the adapter-boundary design
(/home/drawal/rl/devreview-artifacts-20260919/adapter-boundary-report-rev4.md). Second of
five on the critical path F1 -> F2 -> F3 -> F4 -> F5a.

WHAT IT DOES. Today one overloaded request type serves two jobs, with a mode flag choosing
between them. Split it in two (Revision 4 section 3.3):

    @dataclass(frozen=True)
    class SourceRequest:                 # 4 fields - one batch of one query
        descriptor: Mapping[str, Any]
        continuation: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None
        limit: int = 0
        contains: Optional[str] = None

    @dataclass(frozen=True)
    class TerminalRequest:               # the walk reached its end
        descriptor: Mapping[str, Any]
        continuation: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]]
        contains: Optional[str] = None
        batches_read: int = 0            # see OPEN QUESTION below
        distinct_uids: int = 0

Batch response: `rows` (required), `continuation` (optional; absent means the adapter
offers no resume point). Terminal response: `complete` (optional bool), `incomplete_reason`
(optional, passed through verbatim).

THE FOUR FRAMEWORK RULES this task writes into the contract (Revision 4 section 3.3):
(1) one backend operation per callback; (2) the terminal callback is framework-issued, at
most once per walk terminal, and is never charged against MAX_RESOLVER_CALLS_PER_FETCH;
(3) a batch callback may not claim completeness - `complete` and `incomplete_reason` on a
batch response are ignored; (4) absent is incomplete.

Revision 3's cooperative `SourceRequest.allowance` is deleted and is not to be
reintroduced: an allowance of two operations per callback permits 2N backend operations
across N callbacks, and Revision 4 section 2.2 measures that reaching exactly 2.00x in
both capped walk shapes - the shapes where today's code makes zero reconciliation calls.

ANCHORS, re-verified against the working tree at 1c6992e (Revision 4's paging.py numbers
are stale by +23/+24 in this region, non-uniformly):

  - paging.py:1202-1219 - today's SourceRequest. Six fields: descriptor, start, limit,
    contains, filter_columns, count_only. `count_only` (:1219) is the mode flag that turns
    a batch request into a reconciliation request; its only producer is _reconcile at
    paging.py:1747-1758.
  - paging.py:1222 _call_resolver, :1249 _coerce_rows, :1335 _coerce_row_count,
    :1372 _columns_of - the response-coercion layer, accepted keys rows/total/count/columns.
  - paging.py:257 register_resolver, :272 unregister_resolver, :276 registered_resolvers,
    :280 resolver_for - the registry is process-local, never persisted, already generic.
    NO CHANGE proposed.

HONEST SIZING, because two previous revisions died on overreach. This is not a net
reduction in request-side surface: today 1 type / 6 fields, Revision 3 1 type / 5 fields,
Revision 4 2 types / 9 fields. The defensible claim is that an overloaded mode flag is
replaced by an explicit second callback at a cost of four net fields, buying a structural
guarantee that placement and count of the reconciliation are facts of the framework's
control flow rather than an adapter promise. Revision 4's section 0 sentence calling this
"a reduction in interface surface, not an addition" should be amended (see F8).

BLOCKED BY fix-iq53.2.4. Condition 2 of the owner's acceptance is a protocol rule this
task must carry: an empty batch terminates the walk regardless of any continuation
offered. Without it the framework's only independent termination condition is gone and an
adapter returning an empty batch with a continuation never terminates.

OPEN QUESTION, NOT AGREED SCOPE. The independent review of Revision 4 recommends dropping
TerminalRequest.batches_read (5 fields -> 4) on the grounds that nothing consumes it:
_reconcile does not use a batch count today, the IDO resolver does not use one, and the
only named consumer is the framework-side telemetry event, which does not need the number
to cross the boundary. distinct_uids is justified and stays - the completeness rule is
literally countOnly == distinct_uids and the dedup is framework-side. THE OWNER HAS NOT
RULED ON THIS. Do not drop the field on this note alone; get a decision first.
acceptance_criteria:
1. SourceRequest has exactly four fields and carries no mode flag; TerminalRequest exists
as a separate frozen dataclass; `count_only` and `population_only` are gone from the
request surface.
2. The contract text states all four framework rules verbatim, including rule 3 (a batch
callback may not claim completeness) and rule 4 (absent is incomplete).
3. The contract text states the fix-iq53.2.4 backstop: an empty batch terminates the walk
regardless of any continuation offered.
4. A batch response carrying `complete` or `incomplete_reason` is demonstrably ignored, by
test.
5. The registry (paging.py:257-282) is unchanged.
6. The TerminalRequest.batches_read question is answered by the owner, in writing, before
the type is frozen - either a consumer is named or the field is dropped.
notes:
Container: this task is one of F1-F8 of the framework split held by fix-iq53.2.1. It is filed as a sibling of that container rather than a child because bd treats a parent-child edge to a non-epic parent as a blocker, which would make every F-task permanently invisible to bd ready. The container relationship is expressed as dependency edges from fix-iq53.2.1 onto F1-F8 instead, so fix-iq53.2.1 cannot be closed or shipped before its constituent work lands.
OWNER RULING 2026-09-19 on TerminalRequest.batches_read: OMIT IT. Keep the field out; add a defaulted 'batches_read: int = 0' later if I4 (ido-0rk.2.1.4) turns out to need it. Rationale: appending a defaulted field to a frozen dataclass later breaks nothing, while removing a field from a contract adapters have been written against IS a contract break -- so omission is the reversible choice regardless of who is right on the merits. Also: distinct_uids has a named consumer (IDO's rule is literally countOnly == distinct_uids, with dedup framework-side); no equivalent consumer was found for batches_read in _reconcile or resolve_relation_view, and the telemetry event in Rev 4 section 3.5 is framework-side and does not need the number to cross the boundary. TerminalRequest ships at four fields: descriptor, continuation, contains, distinct_uids. This resolves the open question; it is no longer a blocker on freezing F2.
close_reason: F2 landed in 9de144d. SourceRequest at four fields (descriptor, continuation, limit, contains); TerminalRequest added at four (descriptor, continuation, contains, distinct_uids) with batches_read omitted per owner ruling. Mode flag gone. A batch response may not claim completeness -- documented invariant with a test where an adapter claims complete:True on every batch and the page still reports the terminal's answer. Focused sweep 874 passed / 10 skipped / 0 failed exit 0; 451 historical stores re-verified byte-identical with zero sidecars created. Not pushed.

title: F3 - Drive the walk from a stored opaque continuation and allocate batch ordinals
description:
F3 of the framework task split in Revision 4 section 8 of the adapter-boundary design
(/home/drawal/rl/devreview-artifacts-20260919/adapter-boundary-report-rev4.md). Third of
five on the critical path F1 -> F2 -> F3 -> F4 -> F5a.

WHAT IT DOES. The walk currently computes its next read by offset arithmetic it owns.
Under the new boundary the framework stops doing arithmetic on a backend's coordinate
system: it hands back whatever opaque continuation the adapter last returned, and
allocates its own monotonic batch ordinal for storage. Two code paths must change
together - the live extension and the cold rebuild - because a walk that resumes in a new
process must land in the same place as one that never stopped.

ANCHORS, re-verified against the working tree at 1c6992e (Revision 4's paging.py numbers
are stale by +23/+24 in this region, non-uniformly):

  - paging.py:1513-1676 _extend_walk, ~163 lines. Loop becomes keyed on the adapter's
    continuation rather than on an offset. Offset arithmetic to remove: :1564 the limit
    from descriptor page_size; :1570 the stored-page lookup by start_offset; :1633 the
    put_page call passing start_offset=start; :1666 `walk["next_offset"] = start + limit`.
  - paging.py:1382-1487 _walk_records, ~105 lines - the cold rebuild. :1413 derives the
    resume origin from the descriptor's start_offset; :1432 reads page["start_offset"] as
    the terminal; :1440-1442 advances next_offset from a stored page's start_offset plus
    limit_requested. All three become ordinal/continuation reads.
  - paging.py:1450-1466 - verdict rehydration. Revision 4 section 2.4 measures that a cold
    resume of a completed walk currently costs ZERO callbacks and still serves every row.
    The batch_index rename must not break this; it is the ido-1r0 regression the
    rehydration exists to prevent.
  - Dedup that must survive byte-for-byte: rebuild at paging.py:1434-1439, live at
    paging.py:1662-1665. `walk["seen"]` is framework-side and stays framework-side; its
    count is what F4 hands the adapter as TerminalRequest.distinct_uids.

BATCH ORDINAL. `batch_index` is a framework-allocated monotonic ordinal, 0 for the
producer's own page. The storage side of that is F5a; this task is the allocator and the
resume logic that consumes it.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Neither _extend_walk nor _walk_records performs arithmetic on a backend offset; both
resume from the stored opaque continuation.
2. Batch ordinals are allocated monotonically from 0, with 0 reserved for the producer's
own page.
3. A cold resume of a completed walk still costs zero callbacks and still serves every
row - asserted by a test, not by inspection.
4. Uid dedup is unchanged on both the rebuild and the live path, and distinct_uids is
available to the terminal callback.
5. The walk survives the four measured shapes (normal, filtered, exhausted, capped) with
the same batch-read counts Revision 4 section 2.1 records.
notes: Container: this task is one of F1-F8 of the framework split held by fix-iq53.2.1. It is filed as a sibling of that container rather than a child because bd treats a parent-child edge to a non-epic parent as a blocker, which would make every F-task permanently invisible to bd ready. The container relationship is expressed as dependency edges from fix-iq53.2.1 onto F1-F8 instead, so fix-iq53.2.1 cannot be closed or shipped before its constituent work lands.
close_reason: F3 landed in 9de144d. The walk runs on the adapter's own resume point: _extend_walk no longer mints {offset: start} and reads continuation out of the stored batch AFTER the write, so an unstorable batch moves neither ordinal nor resume point. _walk_records rebuilds both from storage. Ordinals via PRODUCER_BATCH_INDEX=0 and walk[next_batch_index]. A batch with rows and no continuation now ends the walk after those rows, saving the empty probe. Focused sweep 874 passed / 10 skipped / 0 failed exit 0; 451 historical stores re-verified byte-identical with zero sidecars created. Not pushed.

title: F4 - Replace _reconcile with a framework-issued uncharged terminal callback
description:
F4 of the framework task split in Revision 4 section 8 of the adapter-boundary design
(/home/drawal/rl/devreview-artifacts-20260919/adapter-boundary-report-rev4.md). Fourth of
five on the critical path F1 -> F2 -> F3 -> F4 -> F5a. This is the task that actually
moves the completeness judgment across the boundary.

WHAT IT DOES. Delete _reconcile and issue the F2 TerminalRequest at the same call site.
The framework keeps deciding WHEN and HOW OFTEN it calls out; the adapter decides WHAT the
terminal check is and WHAT it concludes - the countOnly, the distinct-uid comparison, the
origin rule and the reason words. Placement and count stop being a cooperative promise and
become facts of the framework's own control flow, in exactly the sense they are facts
today: the framework does not call, therefore the call does not happen.

ANCHORS, re-verified against the working tree at 1c6992e (Revision 4's paging.py numbers
are stale by +23/+24 in this region, non-uniformly):

  - paging.py:1710-1792 _reconcile, ~83 lines. DELETED.
  - paging.py:1669-1673 - its single call site, guarded by `if walk["complete"]:`. The
    terminal callback is issued here, at the same moment.
  - paging.py:1651-1659 - the terminal-empty branch, the only place walk["complete"] is
    set on the live path, commented at :1656 as "THE stop condition, and the only one."
    fix-iq53.2.4 requires this backstop be KEPT: an empty batch terminates the walk
    regardless of any continuation offered.
  - The three guards that make a second terminal unreachable and must keep composing:
    the `reconciled` early return at paging.py:1547-1552 (set by _settle_walk at :1795-1799),
    the `complete` early return at paging.py:1553-1554, and the fetch_page fill-loop break
    at paging.py:2034-2041, which breaks on walk["complete"] or any walk stop_reason.
  - UNCHARGED. MAX_RESOLVER_CALLS_PER_FETCH = 8 at paging.py:184; the purse is built once
    per fetch_page at paging.py:2005; _PageCallBudget is paging.py:1491-1510 and its
    docstring says the count-only reconciliation is not charged at paging.py:1496-1497;
    the debit happens before the call at paging.py:1583; exhaustion is a typed non-fatal
    stop at paging.py:1576-1580. The terminal must not touch the purse.
  - THE UNSETTLED-TERMINAL RETRY MUST BE REPRODUCED, NOT FIXED. countonly_error returns
    without settling at paging.py:1765-1769; countonly_unavailable at :1770-1773. Revision
    4 section 2.4 measures the consequence: fetch 0 is BBBC, then each later fetch is a
    bare C - one callback, zero batch reads. A "once ever" hook would make a transient
    failure permanent.
  - paging.py:1774 `distinct = len(walk["records"])` - the number the framework computes
    today and hands across as TerminalRequest.distinct_uids.
  - paging.py:1795-1799 _settle_walk and :1802-1835 _record_walk_terminal - persist the
    adapter's `complete` and stop_reason, minus count_only.
  - paging.py:1452-1457 - the rule "discard a verdict whose count_only is NULL" becomes
    "a row with no `complete` decision is not a verdict".
  - paging.py:1850-1860 _STOP_REASON_NOTES - the four countonly_*/offset_origin_not_zero
    entries (:1854-1857) move to the adapter; `completeness_not_claimed` is added. This is
    the single new word in the whole design.
  - paging.py:2106-2115 walk_can_continue, with the stop-reason allowlist at :2114, and
    the fall-through at :2130-2132 producing continuation="source-incomplete",
    next_cursor=None. NO CHANGE IS NEEDED: the allowlist is positive, so any new stop word
    falls outside it automatically. Revision 4 section 4.1's claim of zero new code here
    is correct.
  - paging.py:1782-1792 - the result_handle_reconciled event. Keep it, substitute the
    adapter's values, add the framework's own batches_read and terminal_callbacks. This is
    telemetry, not a bound, and must not be described as one.

ONE LOOSE CLAIM IN REVISION 4 TO NOT COPY. Section 4.1 says the no-resume-point page
"serves every stored row, offers no cursor". paging.py:2117 is
`if remaining > 0 or walk_can_continue:`, so intermediate pages of a stalled walk DO get a
cursor to page through already-stored rows; only the final page offers none. The section
4.1 example is a final page, so the example is right and the prose is loose.

WHAT THE FRAMEWORK STILL CANNOT ENFORCE, and must not pretend to. How many backend
operations happen inside one callback is invisible across the boundary - equally true
today. That is a tested invariant (F7 framework-side, I6 workflow-side), never a framework
check.
acceptance_criteria:
1. _reconcile is deleted; the terminal callback is issued at paging.py:1669-1673, the same
call site and the same moment.
2. The terminal callback is never charged against MAX_RESOLVER_CALLS_PER_FETCH, asserted by
a test that pins total callbacks per fetch at 9 (8 charged + 1 uncharged).
3. At most one terminal callback per walk terminal, and it is always the last callback of
its fetch. A capped walk makes zero terminal callbacks.
4. The unsettled-terminal retry is reproduced exactly: after a terminal that claims
nothing, each later fetch costs one callback and zero batch reads.
5. An empty batch terminates the walk regardless of any continuation offered
(fix-iq53.2.4).
6. `completeness_not_claimed` is added to _STOP_REASON_NOTES; the four countonly_* /
offset_origin_not_zero words are no longer framework-owned; the walk_can_continue allowlist
at paging.py:2106-2115 is unmodified and the new word falls outside it.
7. The framework never upgrades an unclaimed walk to complete, and a verdict row with no
`complete` decision is not treated as a verdict.
8. The page header rendered by rendering.py:51-78 is byte-identical to today for every
shape that does not involve a dropped descriptor field.

title: Contract must state that an empty batch terminates the walk regardless of any continuation offered
description:
Condition 2 of the owner's 2026-09-19 acceptance of Revision 4 of the adapter-boundary design (/home/drawal/rl/devreview-artifacts-20260919/adapter-boundary-report-rev4.md). Must be settled before F2 freezes the request/response protocol.

THE PROBLEM. Today the framework recognises exhaustion independently of the adapter. Verified at 10e6aae, fastworkflow/result_handles/paging.py:1656-1659 is the single place walk["complete"] is set on the live path, and the source comments it as:

        # THE stop condition, and the only one.
        walk["complete"] = True
        walk["terminal_offset"] = start
        break

Revision 4 section 3.2 swaps this: the framework is to recognise the terminal "by an absent continuation rather than an empty batch". Termination then depends entirely on the adapter eventually omitting `continuation`, and the framework's only independent termination condition is gone.

THE UNSPECIFIED CASE. Section 3.6 specifies four failure modes - an adapter that cannot finish a batch, a terminal check that fails, a terminal callback that raises, and the framework never upgrading an unclaimed walk. It does not specify an adapter that returns an empty batch while still offering a continuation. Under the contract as written that walk never terminates. Within a single fetch the purse bounds it (MAX_RESOLVER_CALLS_PER_FETCH = 8, paging.py:184), but across fetches nothing does, so it burns up to 8 backend calls per fetch indefinitely while every page looks like legitimate progress. That is the ido-1r0 failure mode in a new costume - the same thing Revision 4 section 4.2 correctly rejects the "restart" option for.

THE FIX. One explicit sentence in the contract: an empty batch terminates the walk regardless of any continuation offered. It keeps the existing safety net rather than trading it away, preserves today's behaviour exactly, and costs the contract nothing.

NOTE ON A RELATED, SEPARATE ITEM (not in scope here, recorded so it is not lost). Revision 4 also preserves today's unsettled-terminal retry: when the count is unavailable or errors, the terminal is left unsettled and re-attempted on every later fetch, forever, at one callback and zero batch reads each. Revision 4 treats that as a property to reproduce rather than fix. It is the status quo and is cheap, but the "exactly one reconciliation per walk" headline is only true on the happy path; on a transiently broken portal the real profile is unbounded reconciliations per handle lifetime. The owner's acceptance inherits this behaviour; whether to change it is a separate decision and the new contract is the moment when changing it would be free.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The contract text (section 3.6 or the F2 protocol section) states explicitly that an empty batch terminates the walk regardless of any continuation offered.
2. F4's terminal recognition implements it: an empty batch marks the walk terminal even when the batch response carries a non-null continuation.
3. An F7 regression test drives an adapter that returns an empty batch together with a continuation and asserts the walk terminates within that fetch rather than continuing to re-fetch, and that the page reports the terminal rather than looking like progress.
4. Done before F2 (SourceRequest at 4 fields plus TerminalRequest) is frozen.
close_reason: Contract rule written in four places and enforced at the boundary: _batch_continuation returns None whenever rows is empty, so an empty batch's continuation cannot survive to reach the walk. Empty-batch and absent-continuation terminals now agree by construction rather than by a guard F3 had to remember.     paging.py:2213), which at paging.py:2222 renders:

     undercount already flagged as revision-1 correction 7, so the inventory has now been wrong in
