title: ConversationStore.update_conversation is unreachable dead code and still carries the self-collision defect
description:
Discovered independently by the fix-dzs.2 and fix-dzs.3 agents (2026-08-13) while
fixing the sibling defect.

`ConversationStore.update_conversation` (`fastworkflow/run_fastapi_mcp/conversation_store.py`)
calls `_ensure_unique_topic` WITHOUT the `exclude_conversation_id` argument that
fix-dzs.2 added to its two siblings, so it still has the self-collision defect: a
rewrite with an unchanged topic oscillates between `'Topic'` and `'Topic 1'`.
Verified by the fix-dzs.2 agent: saving `'Billing Question'` and then calling
`update_conversation` with the same topic yields `'Billing Question 1'`.

WHY IT IS NOT URGENT. `rg` finds no callers anywhere in the repo — only the
definition. It is unreachable today, so this is latent, not live. fix-dzs.3's
blank-candidate guard also protects it from the `' 1'` empty-topic state, so the
only remaining defect is the suffix oscillation on a non-blank rewrite.

DECIDE ONE OF TWO, both one-line-ish:
1. Pass `exclude_conversation_id=conv_id`, exactly as its two siblings now do, so
   the method is correct if a caller ever appears.
2. Delete the method, since nothing calls it and `update_conversation_topic_summary`
   plus `save_conversation_turns` / `append_conversation_turns` cover the live
   paths between them.

Prefer (2) if you are confident no external consumer imports the store directly;
prefer (1) if the store is treated as a public surface. Note the repo rule against
deleting tests — check whether any test exercises it before removing it.

ALSO IN SCOPE, two pre-existing nits in the same file both agents flagged and
deliberately left alone:
- `from re import I` (near the top) is an unused stray import.
- `normalized_candidate` in `_ensure_unique_topic` was computed and never read
  until fix-dzs.3's guard started using it; confirm it is now genuinely used and
  that the `# Normalize for comparison` comment still describes what happens.

ACCEPTANCE. Either the method is correct or it is gone; `rg` confirms no caller
was broken; the fix-dzs.2 and fix-dzs.3 tests in
`tests/test_conversation_topic_labeling.py` still pass.
close_reason: Took option (1), the conservative one: update_conversation now passes exclude_conversation_id=conv_id like its two siblings, so it is correct if a caller ever appears. Did NOT delete it - that needs the 'is ConversationStore a public surface?' judgment, which is design input. Also removed the stray 'from re import I'. The normalized_candidate nit resolved itself: fix-dzs.3's blank guard now uses it.

title: Streaming end-of-stream waits on lazy topic generation in run_owned_turn
description:
Discovered while implementing fix-dzs.6 (2026-08-13); reported by that agent as a
deliberate trade, not an oversight.

`run_owned_turn` (`fastworkflow/run_fastapi_mcp/turns.py`) is the lifecycle for
`POST /invoke_agent_stream`. The lazy-labeling hook runs as the last act of that
task, and the streaming endpoint's `owned_turn` wrapper emits its end-of-stream
sentinel only after `run_owned_turn` returns. So the response BODY can stay open
for up to one topic-generation round trip (bounded at
`LLM_CONVERSATION_STORE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, default 12s x 2 attempts).

WHAT IS AND IS NOT AFFECTED. The client's actual answer is not delayed: the
terminal `output` event is emitted by the work function well before the hook
runs. Only EOF is late. A client that reads until the sentinel therefore holds a
connection open longer than it needs to; a client that acts on the terminal event
sees no difference.

WHY IT WAS ACCEPTED. Fixing it properly means plumbing the appended-turn count
out of `run_owned_turn` and adding a second call site in the streaming endpoint,
after the sentinel. That is a wider change to the turn lifecycle than the labeling
work warranted, and the alternative (labeling before `trim_live_sessions`) would
hold the session cache over target for the length of an LLM call instead.

SCOPE IF PICKED UP. Move the hook for the streaming path to after the sentinel is
emitted, keeping the fix-dzs.6 R7 properties intact: the channel must not be
counted busy by `wait_for_active_turns_to_complete` while the LLM call runs, the
runtime must not be retired or closed underneath it (the labeling path reaches
only the durable store, never `runtime.execution_context` — preserve that), and
the client must not wait on it.

ACCEPTANCE. A streaming turn's EOF arrives without waiting on topic generation,
and the fix-dzs.6 tests in `tests/test_conversation_lazy_labeling.py` still pass
unchanged.
close_reason: Fixed with an optional on_done callback on run_owned_turn, awaited once the turn is observably DONE and before the trim and the label. The streaming endpoint passes finish_stream, which emits any terminal error event and then the sentinel, so the response body ends as soon as the turn does. Cheaper than the bead's plan (plumb turns_appended out, second label call site): one label call site, no new field, ~6 lines of lifecycle change. owned_turn keeps its finally sentinel as the guarantee - a duplicate is harmless since the drain loop stops at the first, whereas a missing one hangs the client. Ordering hazard found and handled: owned_turn used to emit its error event AFTER run_owned_turn returned, so a naive early sentinel would have swallowed it; on_done is deliberately placed after the except blocks so a caller can still read execn.error. WHY IT MATTERED MORE THAN FILED: invoke_agent, the MCP-exposed tool, IS this streaming endpoint (operation_id invoke_agent maps to /invoke_agent_stream; mcp_specific excludes rest_invoke_agent instead), and fastapi-mcp reads the whole stream as the tool result - so an MCP agent paid the generation in its tool call on every labeled turn. Also removes a failure mode where a client with a short idle-read timeout fails a turn whose answer it already received. Closed a coverage gap too: run_owned_turn's labeling had NO test (only _run_turn's did). 4 new tests; the EOF one verified discriminating - moving on_done after the label fails exactly that test and nothing else. 188 pass across the affected suites.

title: R12: ensure_topic_and_summary spec gaps — no no-turns guard, and a missing conv record raises ValueError
description:
NICE-TO-HAVE hardening of the helper specified in gh-65 implementation note 2 and
built in fix-dzs.6. Two unhandled cases; both are cheap to close and neither is
worth blocking the feature on.

GAP 1 — no "no turns" guard. gh-65 specifies the helper as: no-op if
active_conversation_id == 0 or (not force and topic already set); load turn
summaries via get_conversation_summaries; generate; update. There is no guard for
an EMPTY summary list, so with force=True the helper would hand the LLM "[]" and
store whatever it invents. /new_conversation guards this today with
`if turns := _conversation_turns_for_summary(runtime)` (__main__.py:1517); the
helper spec drops it. Add the guard to the helper so the guard is not
per-call-site.

GAP 2 — a reserved-but-unwritten conversation raises. update_conversation_topic_summary
raises ValueError(f"Conversation {conv_id} not found") when conv:{id} is absent
(conversation_store.py:265-268). That state is real: /new_conversation reserves the
next id (__main__.py:1535) and no conv record exists until the first
append_conversation_turns. _conversation_turns_for_summary falls through to
in-memory history when get_conversation_summaries returns empty
(__main__.py:325-330), so a channel with in-memory turns and a freshly reserved id
reaches update_conversation_topic_summary with no record and raises — surfacing as
HTTP 500 from /new_conversation, or as the "Failed to finalize conversation" line
at shutdown today.
  The chat-turn path is safe by construction (save_conversation_incremental's
append creates the record before the helper could run), so this is reachable
mainly via the rotate and the old shutdown paths. Decide: create the record, or
no-op with a WARNING. Recommendation: no-op — the helper's job is labeling, not
conversation creation, and fix-dzs.1 keeps the durable-save fallback where
creation belongs.

SCOPE. Both guards inside ensure_topic_and_summary, so no call site has to
remember them. No store schema change.

ACCEPTANCE.
- force=True with zero recorded turns makes no LLM call.
- The helper against a reserved-but-unwritten conversation neither raises nor
  fabricates a record.
- /new_conversation immediately after a rotate, with in-memory turns present,
  returns 200.
notes:
SCOPE REDUCED 2026-08-13 by fix-dzs.6, which landed the lazy-fill helper.

GAP 1 (no no-turns guard) is CLOSED. ensure_topic_and_summary in run_fastapi_mcp/utils.py returns early when the durable turn count is 0 and again when the projected summaries list is empty, so no call site has to remember it and force=True cannot hand the model an empty list.

GAP 2 (reserved-but-unwritten conversation raising ValueError) is closed for every LAZY trigger: they no-op on active_conversation_id == 0 and read the durable record via get_conversation_label_state, so update_conversation_topic_summary is never reached without a record. It is NOT closed for /new_conversation's defensive active_conversation_id == 0 branch, which was deliberately left as-is because that branch CREATES a conversation rather than labeling one - which is the boundary this issue itself recommends keeping.

WHAT REMAINS: decide whether /new_conversation's create-on-missing-record branch stays, and add a regression test for the rotate-immediately-after-rotate path (POST /new_conversation twice with in-memory turns present but a freshly reserved id). Re-scope or close as already-satisfied after checking that path against the current code.
close_reason: GAP 1 was already closed by fix-dzs.6 (no-turns guard inside the helper). GAP 2 fixed by persist-then-label in /new_conversation, which is neither option the bead offered - both were wrong. No-op-with-a-WARNING would let the rotate clear history and LOSE the unpersisted turns; creating a bare record inside the labeling helper puts conversation creation in a function whose job is labeling. Instead /new_conversation now calls save_conversation_incremental before labeling (the same chokepoint fix-dzs.1 uses for shutdown): it reserves the id when there is none, appends what is missing, and creates the record, so the ValueError is impossible AND the turns are durable before the rotate clears the history holding them. Probe evidence: in the reserved-but-unwritten state the old code called the LLM, THEN raised ValueError: Conversation N not found, so the rotate that would have cleaned the state up was the one unavailable operation and each retry bought another provider call. Also corrected the 500 message, which claimed 'Topic/summary generation failed' (generation had succeeded; the write failed) and 'no turns were lost' (they were not durable) - now 'Could not label the conversation ... Its turns are durably recorded', which is only true BECAUSE the persist runs first. Regression test added to test_conversation_lazy_labeling.py, verified discriminating: without the fix it is a 500 with ValueError. 148 pass across the affected suites.

title: enablecache cache key collides on equal-repr / kwargs order
description: Out of scope for speedict→sqlite migration (fix-lvl). enablecache keys with str(args)+str(kwargs), which collides for arguments with equal repr and is sensitive to kwargs ordering. Improve with a stable hash (e.g. json.dumps(args/kwargs, sort_keys=True, default=str) or hashlib) when someone next touches the decorator.

title: File follow-up: enablecache key collision (str args/kwargs)
description: Out-of-scope note from design §4 Step 1: enablecache cache key is str(args)+str(kwargs), which collides for equal-repr args and is kwargs-order sensitive. Track as separate improvement; do not fix in migration.
close_reason: Closed

title: v2.29.1 flipped the DSPy disk cache on under a CVE-floors subject
description:
NOT NECESSARILY WRONG -- filed so the decision is visible rather than buried.

Commit 38ceceb's subject is 'raise CVE floors, local scanners, OpenVEX for diskcache'. It also, in fastworkflow/run_fastapi_mcp/server_memory.py:
  - flipped enable_disk_cache=False -> True (capped at 1 GiB)
  - INVERTED the drift check in check_policy_in_force(), from 'disk cache re-enabled' to 'disk cache disabled'
  - removed the comment stating the disk cache was off BECAUSE DSPy's is pickle-backed and 30 GB is not a sane container default, replacing that rationale with an OpenVEX acceptance of CVE-2025-69872.

The security rationale is therefore reversed, and the drift check now asserts the opposite invariant. That may well be the right call -- 1 GiB is bounded and OpenVEX is a real answer to the pickle concern -- but a behaviour change to a server memory policy is not what the subject line describes, and it is the direct cause of the one hard test failure in the v2.29.1 run (a probe that assumed a cold cache).

DO: nothing to the code unless you disagree with the flip. This exists so that anyone reading server_memory.py's history finds the decision, and so the reversal of the stated security rationale is on the record rather than only in a diff.
notes: Accepted as-is: keep DSPy disk cache ON (1 GiB cap + OpenVEX for CVE-2025-69872). No code change.
close_reason: Closed

title: Deprecations that will break on the next dependency bump
description:
Surfaced by the v2.29.1 upgrade run (dspy 3.3, transformers 5.14, pandas 3.0). None is broken today; each has a named removal.

1. StarletteDeprecationWarning: 'Using httpx with starlette.testclient is deprecated; install httpx2 instead'. Affects EVERY TestClient test, which is most of the FastAPI suite.
2. FieldValidationInfo imported at fastworkflow/command_directory.py:8 -- deprecated in Pydantic V2, REMOVED in V3.
3. ast.Str and elt.s at fastworkflow/build/documentation_generator.py:91-92 -- REMOVED in Python 3.14.
4. tokenizers WordPiece.__init__ deprecation.

Worth doing together rather than one at a time when each breaks: they are all mechanical, and the failure mode for 2 and 3 is an ImportError/AttributeError at import, which given that 'import fastworkflow' pulls the whole stack means the package stops importing at all rather than degrading.
notes:
## Completed 2026-08-08

### Fixed
1. FieldValidationInfo → ValidationInfo in fastworkflow/command_directory.py (kept).
2. ast.Str/elt.s → ast.Constant/elt.value in fastworkflow/build/documentation_generator.py (kept).
3. httpx2>=2.0.0 added: optional main dep + server/fastapi extras + test group; poetry lock refreshed; locked httpx2==2.9.1 (+ httpcore2, truststore). Starlette TestClient httpx deprecation cleared (0 httpx-related warnings).

### Won't-fix (documented)
4. tokenizers WordPiece.__init__ deprecation: originates in upstream transformers BertTokenizer (tokenization_bert.py) when AutoTokenizer loads BERT vocab.txt. We do not construct WordPiece. No in-repo hack; wait for transformers to migrate to WordPiece.from_file.

### Tests
- test_command_directory.py + test_command_directory_cme.py + test_build/test_readme_generation.py: 5 passed (prior pass).
- test_fastapi_service.py: 31 passed; TestClient smoke shows no Starlette httpx deprecation.
close_reason: Closed

title: Dependabot #99 torch.jit.script — already on patched 2.13.0
description:
## Finding
Dependabot alert **#99** (Low): PyTorch `torch.jit.script` memory corruption (GHSA-rrmf-rvhw-rf47 / CVE-2025-3000).

## Analysis
- Advisory: affected ≤2.12.1; **first patched 2.13.0**
- Locked: `torch==2.13.0+cpu` (pyproject `^2.7.1`, source pytorch-cpu)
- Local pip-audit after CVE floors does **not** report torch
- Alert likely stale relative to current lock, or Dependabot does not treat `2.13.0+cpu` local version as satisfying 2.13.0

## Recommendation
1. After 2.29.1 poetry.lock is on default branch, wait for Dependabot re-scan.
2. If #99 remains open, dismiss as **fixed in 2.13.0** (note +cpu local tag).
3. No version bump required unless a newer advisory appears.
4. Reachability: we use torch for intent-model training/inference, not typically `torch.jit.script` on untrusted models — Low severity matches.

## Effort
None for code; dismiss-only after push.
notes: No code change: lock already torch 2.13.0+cpu. Remaining work is Dependabot dismiss after push.
close_reason: Closed

title: DEFAULT_MIN_POOL_MULTIPLE sits outside every digest
description:
DISCOVERED FROM fix-6r5, and it is that bug's exact shape one level out.

DomainConditionedPersonaSource.rows computes its pool floor from self._min_pool_multiple, which defaults to the module constant DEFAULT_MIN_POOL_MULTIPLE. Editing that constant changes the persona pool a command is generated from without changing the TEXT of any digested function, so it invalidates nothing -- a developer retunes it, retrains, and silently gets the old personas back.

fix-6r5 closed the hole for the source's own methods by digesting them via reflection. This is the residue: MODULE CONSTANTS READ BY DIGESTED FUNCTIONS are still invisible.

Low severity today (no production caller overrides it), but note the general shape rather than patching the one constant: any constant a digested function reads has this property, and the reflection approach fix-6r5 introduced does not reach them. A general fix would digest the constants a function closes over, or move tunables into the source's fingerprint().
close_reason: Fixed narrowly, as scoped. The constant is folded into pool_source_digest as a named NAME=value string -- no hash(), no repr() -- so it stays byte-stable across processes; the existing three-PYTHONHASHSEED fresh-process test still passes. It goes in the BASE pool_source_digest because subclasses are forbidden from overriding it, which is harmless: plain PersonaHub never reaches the digest, and both sources that do (DomainConditioned via rows, AppPersonaSource via notes) genuinely read the constant. The general shape -- any module constant a digested function reads, unreachable by source-text reflection -- is named in the docstring as explicitly out of scope. Mutation: removing the fold collapses the digest to the identical value and makes the cache reuse the old entry, failing both new tests.

title: Two stores' reap 'reclaimed' now mean different things
description:
DISCOVERED FROM fix-xm1, which changed one of them.

SessionStateStore.reap: reclaimed now counts CONFIRMED removals, with a separate failures count for blobs that were selected but could not be removed.

CheckpointStore.reap: increments reclaimed_channels BEFORE attempting _retire_directory, and counts errors separately in failures. So its reclaimed is a count of INTENTIONS.

Two stores, the same field name, two meanings -- and the difference only shows up when something fails, which is exactly when an operator is reading the number. Someone comparing 'reclaimed' across the two namespaces to judge whether retention is working gets an answer that is right for one and optimistic for the other.

CheckpointStore's is at least accompanied by a failure count, so it is not silent. But the inconsistency should be resolved deliberately rather than left as an artifact of which one got fixed first. Aligning CheckpointStore to count confirmations is the obvious direction; the alternative (documenting both as intentions) is worse, because fix-xm1 fixed a bug that existed precisely because the count was an intention.

Also: run_fastapi_mcp/__main__.py's periodic reaper logs reclaimed, protected and unreadable but not the new failures. reap warns per unremovable blob and names the path, so nothing is silent, but a one-line aggregate beside the unreadable warning would surface it in the same place.
close_reason: Fixed, and reproduced before fixing: a plain file planted where the reclaim holding area belongs makes _retire_directory refuse, and a single unreclaimable channel then reported reclaimed=1, failures=1, 2.5 KB freed -- while still being loadable. The count AND the byte figure were both wrong in the one situation an operator reads them. Counting now happens after the flip, gating reclaimed, both byte totals and reclaimed_keys on what _retire_directory confirms left the namespace; a dry run still counts the projection. ReapReport's docstring states the same contract as PendingReapOutcome, including that reclaimed + failures can be less than the selection when another process got there first. On the failures question: it was already populated from two places (channel retirement and _reap_quarantine), so it is documented as spanning both rather than split. The periodic reaper now logs pending.failures beside the unreadable warning. Mutation: confirmed = True restores intention-counting and fails with assert 1 == 0.

title: Spec AR5 says sorting fixed the two-path cache asymmetry; it did not
description:
DISCOVERED FROM fix-4ej.

docs/intent_training_improvements_spec.md section AR5 describes the two-path utterance-cache asymmetry as a DETERMINISM problem that sorting fixes. Sorting fixed the label loss (fix-9mo). It did not fix the coverage floor, because a stable order is still an ORDER -- the floor still took whichever value the first visitor wrote, deterministically.

So the doc of record says a defect is closed that was open until fix-4ej, and attributes the fix to a mechanism that could not have produced it. A reader reasoning from AR5 would conclude the floor is order-independent, which it was not.

Also: R7.2's coverage-floor text should state that core commands are NOT sources for the floor. That is the substantive rule fix-4ej established, and it is the kind of thing a future change would otherwise re-litigate from scratch.

Left alone during fix-4ej because docs/ was outside that workstream's ownership.
close_reason: Fixed, and the correction was already sitting in the code -- model_pipeline_training.py says 'a STABLE order is still an order'. AR5 now carries a correction block splitting the asymmetry into its two consequences, and it turns out sorting fixed NEITHER on its own: fix-9mo's own description says sorting only made the label loss deterministic and the cache fill is what stopped it, while the escalation floor needed fix-4ej removing the dependency rather than stabilising it. R7.2's coverage-floor text now states that core commands are not sources, with the double-counting reason.

title: A large always-include set silently masks coverage-floor defects
description:
DISCOVERED FROM fix-4ej, and it is the reason that bug was findable at all.

select_reserved_rows emits always_include rows regardless of budget. Once |always_include| + coverage >= budget, the coverage floor is INERT -- it stops influencing selection entirely, so any defect in how the floor is derived becomes invisible.

The fix-4ej asymmetry was 4 sources per ancestor context. A workflow whose wildcard command emitted 4 or more non-local rows would have hidden it completely. Today it emits exactly ONE (the humanised command name), which is the only reason the defect showed up in selected rows rather than staying a reporting curiosity.

That is a hair-trigger invariant nobody has written down: widening the wildcard corpus is currently a silent reduction in the observability of this whole defect class.

DO: state the invariant where select_reserved_rows lives, and add a test asserting that always_include stays small relative to a representative budget -- so anyone widening it has to acknowledge the trade rather than discover it later.
close_reason:
Fixed. The invariant is now stated on select_reserved_rows: always-included rows count against budget without being chosen by it, so once len(always_include) + coverage >= budget the fill pass never runs and budget becomes dead input -- and since the coverage floor reaches selection only through budget, a floor defect then survives every test that inspects selected rows. Two tests: one demonstrating the mechanism executably, one guarding the production corpus with a DERIVED bound rather than a chosen number -- the wildcard corpus must stay smaller than the set of non-wildcard core commands, which is the magnitude of the fix-4ej asymmetry it has to leave visible. Today that is 1 against 4. Mutation: widening wildcard.generate_utterances to 4 rows fails the guard.

FOUND WHILE FIXING, and tighter than the issue suggested: at own_row_count == coverage_floor (31 for TodoItem) the budget is ALREADY inert with the single always-include row it has today. The headroom exists only because the cost budget normally dominates the floor.

title: No non-slow test reaches train() end to end
description:
DISCOVERED FROM fix-4ej.

Every caller that drives train() is behind the slow + requires_llm_key markers (added by fix-k0i.42), so the per-context loop inside train() -- which fix-4ej rewired -- is only covered by a tier that is routinely deselected and needs a real API key.

fix-4ej mitigated this deliberately: the shipped decision was extracted into cache_context_command_utterances and select_escalation_rows so a cheap test drives the SAME functions train() calls, leaving roughly 8 lines of glue that were verified by reading. That is a good mitigation, not coverage.

DO: a cheap test that reaches train(), exercises the per-context loop, and stops before model fitting. The value is not this one change -- it is that the loop is where context-by-context decisions are assembled, and it is currently the least-tested code in the training path relative to how often it is edited.
close_reason: Closed

title: turn_key means two different things across the FastAPI surface
description:
DISCOVERED FROM fix-qtq.3.

In a NON-STREAMING response body, turn_key is the TurnRegistry EXECUTION key -- the handle a client polls with GET /turns/{turn_key} after a 202.

In a STREAMING 'output' event, turn_key is TurnOutput.turn_key: the workflow's LOGICAL turn key, which survives an ask_user suspension and spans several executions.

Two distinct key spaces sharing one name on one API. A client that stores the streaming key and polls with it gets a 404; a client that correlates the two silently mismatches across a suspension.

Left alone rather than renamed during fix-qtq because the non-streaming one is the documented 202 polling handle and renaming it is a breaking change. Documented in the endpoint descriptions in the meantime.

FIX: rename one of them (execution_key for the registry handle is the clearer of the two) with a deprecation window, or document them as deliberately distinct with a worked example of correlating a streamed turn to its poll handle.
close_reason: Closed

title: FastAPI spec sections 4, 5 and 11 still describe Topology A
description:
DISCOVERED FROM fix-qtq.9, which corrected the RESPONSE CONTRACT in docs/fastworkflow_fastapi_spec.md but deliberately left the architecture sections alone as out of scope.

Sections 4, 5 and 11 still describe Topology A: ChatSession, command_output_queue, and an 'event: command_output' SSE shape. The runtime has been Topology B since the memory-bounds work -- WorkflowExecutionContext is synchronous and transport-free, FastAPI embeds it per request, and the terminal streaming event now carries a TurnOutput.

A reader following those sections builds against a design that no longer exists, and the parts they describe are the ones an integrator most needs to get right (streaming event shapes and session lifecycle).

Needs its own pass rather than a patch: the sections are structurally about the old topology, not merely stale in their details.
close_reason: Closed

title: Map MCP isError to TurnOutput.success once fastapi-mcp can express it
description:
SUCCESSOR TO fix-qtq.6, which was closed as not-implementable rather than done. The intent is preserved here so it is not lost.

WHAT WAS WANTED: an MCP tool result should carry isError = not TurnOutput.success, so an MCP client can tell a failed turn from a successful one.

WHY IT COULD NOT BE DONE (verified against the installed fastapi-mcp 0.4.0):
- FastApiMCP answers from a private _execute_api_tool returning list[TextContent].
- The MCP SDK sets isError=True only when that handler RAISES.
- _execute_api_tool raises from a response on exactly one condition: 'if 400 <= response.status_code < 600'.

So the only available lever is the HTTP status code. Using it would mean returning 4xx/5xx for a turn that failed -- mapping a turn OUTCOME onto a transport STATUS. That is precisely the conflation the fix-qtq epic exists to remove: a failed turn is a successful HTTP call whose TurnOutput reports the failure. Implementing it that way would have undone the epic while appearing to complete it.

Additionally the streaming tool could not read success at all: its body is a stream.

WHEN THIS BECOMES DOABLE: when fastapi-mcp exposes a way to set isError independently of HTTP status (a result hook, or a documented handler that can construct the CallToolResult), or when we stop routing MCP through fastapi-mcp's auto-conversion. Re-check on the next fastapi-mcp upgrade.

The reasoning is recorded as a TODO in fastworkflow/run_fastapi_mcp/mcp_specific.py and in docs/fastworkflow_fastapi_spec.md, so a future reader hits it at the code rather than only here.
notes: 2026-08-08 re-check: fastapi-mcp still 0.4.0 (PyPI + GitHub main). isError still only via HTTP 4xx/5xx raise in _execute_api_tool. Policy: leave OPEN (blocked); re-check on next fastapi-mcp upgrade. Do not map failed turns to HTTP errors; do not drop fastapi-mcp auto-conversion without explicit design go-ahead.

title: VersionInfo.size_bytes walks every version tree on every list_versions, including on every train
description:
DISCOVERED FROM fix-k0i.50 (a candidate the sweep did not act on because it is a behaviour change, not a deletion).

VersionInfo.size_bytes is populated by _dir_size_bytes, which walks a version's entire directory tree. list_versions builds a VersionInfo per version, so every call walks EVERY version's tree. retain_current_and_previous calls list_versions on every train, so this runs on every training run.

On a multi-gigabyte workflow with several retained versions that is real wasted I/O in the publication path -- which is now also inside the fix-k0i.41 publication lock, so the walk holds the lock longer than it needs to.

Nothing in the training path consumes size_bytes. Its only consumers are format_versions_table and describe_version, which have no production callers (see fix-k0i.50).

FIX: make size_bytes lazy -- a property computed on access, or an opt-in parameter to list_versions defaulted off. Callers that want it are exactly the two display helpers, both of which are already off the hot path.
close_reason:
Fixed by making size_bytes lazy rather than removing it, after verifying the consumer situation rather than assuming it. size_bytes is written only by list_versions and read in exactly ONE place in the repo: an assertion in tests/test_artifact_versioning.py. It is never serialized -- no model_dump/json() call anywhere, no write_manifest caller passes a size, and neither manifest.json nor current.json carries one. Removing it would therefore have broken an existing test, which per instruction is a signal to report rather than act on.

It is now a @property computing _dir_size_bytes on access, with workflow_folderpath carried on the model so it can find its own tree. Verified: isinstance(VersionInfo.size_bytes, property) is True. The existing assertion passes unchanged, and list_versions is now one manifest read plus one shallow listing per version -- so retain_current_and_previous no longer walks every version's tree INSIDE publication_lock, which was the actual cost (fix-k0i.41 put that walk inside the lock).

Deliberately uncached: a version's tree changes when a publish hardlinks a carry-forward in. Returns 0 for a version pruned since it was listed. The module docstring paragraph that said the field should be made lazy now records that it is, and why.

Deleting the field remains possible -- the only thing standing in the way is that one assertion. Not done without approval.

title: Param-example prompt renders repr() of field examples, so a default repr leaks a memory address into the LLM prompt
description:
DISCOVERED FROM fix-k0i.46.

generate_param_examples builds the prompt with ', '.join(repr(ex) for ex in field['examples']). An example object that inherits object.__repr__ therefore renders as '<Foo object at 0x7f...>' INSIDE THE PROMPT SENT TO THE MODEL.

fix-k0i.46 fixed the neighbouring instance of this in the cache KEY (_canonical_digest no longer uses default=repr, because the embedded id() made the key differ every run). The prompt instance is untouched and is arguably worse: an unstable cache key causes a wasted regeneration, whereas an address in the prompt is noise the model conditions on, and it changes every run so the generated examples are irreproducible for reasons invisible in the diff.

FIX: render examples through the same canonicalizer the digest now uses, or require examples to be JSON-native at the Field(examples=[...]) boundary and say so in the command-authoring rule.

Low severity: only bites commands whose Field examples are non-primitive objects, which is unusual.
close_reason:
Fixed, and the fix had to be wider than the issue -- which is the finding.

The issue names ONE route into the prompt (the Examples line, ', '.join(repr(ex) ...)). There are TWO: the prompt also interpolates str(field_annotations), and pydantic's FieldInfo repr nests the repr of everything in json_schema_extra, so the address arrived through that block as well. VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY: str(Input.model_fields) for a field with a non-JSON-native example does contain ' at 0x', and the shipped _address_free strips it. Fixing only the named line would have left the address in the prompt and changed nothing about reproducibility -- a fix that closes the ticket and not the bug.

Examples now render through param_example_cache.run_stable_form -- the same substitutions _canonical_digest reaches -- and are then repr'd, so the rendering stays PYTHON-shaped. That matters: the prompt demands Python output a few lines further down ('None values should be represented as Python None'), so emitting null/true would have contradicted its own instructions. For every JSON-native example the text is character-for-character unchanged, asserted against the old expression.

The annotations block is stripped textually rather than structurally re-rendered, deliberately: re-rendering model_fields would change the prompt for every workflow in existence -- a training-data quality change wearing a determinism fix's clothes.

Narrowing goes through str.__str__ / int.__int__ rather than str() / int(), because str(SomeStrEnum.MEMBER) is 'SomeStrEnum.MEMBER' while json.dumps writes the value -- using str() would have shown the model a name the cache key had never seen.

Did NOT take the 'require JSON-native at the boundary' option, so .claude/rules/command-authoring.md is untouched. Two reasons, both good: an existing test asserts an undigestable command still trains, and raising would have weakened it; and pydantic's native Field(examples=[...]) already IS that strict boundary -- only the json_schema_extra route is permissive.

Invalidates every parameter-example cache entry, unavoidably (editing generate_dspy_examples moves its source_digest). No utterance-cache entry affected.

title: Persona-source row matching is outside the utterance-cache fingerprint
description:
DISCOVERED FROM fix-k0i.43 (which closed the four functions it named; this is the residue).

DomainConditionedPersonaSource.rows and _matches are not digested. Editing which rows a keyword matches changes the persona pool a command is generated from, without invalidating any cache entry -- so a developer tunes the matching, retrains, and silently gets the old personas back.

fix-k0i.43 widened _DIGESTED_GENERATION_SOURCES to derived_seed, select_persona_indices, resolve_personas and PersonaSource.select, which covers the SELECTION algorithm. What is still uncovered is the SOURCE's own matching behaviour.

WHY IT WAS LEFT: closing it properly means digesting the active source's own methods, which makes the fingerprint source-dependent -- a different shape from the current 'digest these named module-level functions' design. That is a design decision, not an oversight.

Low severity while there is effectively one source in use.
close_reason:
Fixed by making the fingerprint source-dependent, but resolved from the source's CLASS rather than its instance state.

The issue framed source-dependence as 'a different shape from the current design'. On inspection that does not hold: the persona_source fingerprint input was ALREADY a function of the installed source, because active_persona_source_label() consults the process-wide source and returns name#fingerprint(). Only a third component was added: name#<content fingerprint>#<pool-code digest>.

The digest comes from PersonaSource.pool_source_digest(), which hashes the source text of every function the concrete class and its bases define, found BY REFLECTION. Reflection rather than a name list is the whole point -- a name list is exactly what left _matches and rows out in the first place: fix-k0i.43 named four functions, two more existed, and nothing failed. Adding DomainConditionedPersonaSource._matches to _DIGESTED_GENERATION_SOURCES was rejected for that reason, and because it would make EVERY workflow regenerate over a keyword filter only a workflow with personas.json can reach.

Determinism verified independently rather than argued: the digest is identical across PYTHONHASHSEED 0/12345/99999 in fresh subprocesses, and is computable from an uninitialised instance -- confirming it reads only type(self), so no instance attribute and no id() can reach it. Ordered by MRO then attribute name so neither __dict__ order nor the hash salt can move it. Properties are unwrapped to .fget and staticmethod/classmethod to .__func__, because inspect.getsource rejects the descriptors and source_digest would otherwise have quietly recorded 'source-unavailable' -- a digest that stops noticing edits while still looking like one.

Invalidation is scoped: utterance-cache entries are invalidated only for workflows WITH a personas.json. A workflow without one keeps its exact existing key, pinned by a test asserting its persona_source input still has no '#'. The default PersonaHub draw keeps label None per decision D6.

title: Empty channel_id reaches the storage layer and now 500s instead of 400ing
description:
DISCOVERED FROM fix-7hn. encode_path_component('') raises ValueError, so a request carrying channel_id='' now fails inside the storage layer rather than at the API boundary.

This is strictly better than what it replaced -- the old _json_path('') returned '_pending.json', ONE SHARED FILE for every empty id, which is the same cross-session defect class fix-7hn just closed. Failing loudly beats silently sharing a bucket.

But it fails in the wrong place. No HTTP handler in run_fastapi_mcp validates that channel_id is non-empty, so the caller sees a 500 (an internal error, implying our bug) where they should see a 400 (their malformed request). It also means the error text is a storage-layer message rather than something an API consumer can act on.

FIX: validate channel_id at the API boundary -- non-empty, and probably a length cap since the encoder hashes beyond the filesystem name limit. The Pydantic request models are the natural home. Keep the ValueError as the backstop; the point is that it should be unreachable from a well-formed request.

Low severity: reachable only by a client sending an empty channel_id, which no normal client does.
close_reason:
Fixed at the boundary with ChannelId = Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1)] on InitializationRequest and GenerateMCPTokenRequest -- the two places a client-supplied channel id enters. SessionData deliberately left alone: its channel_id comes from a JWT this server minted, so constraining it would turn a bad-but-authentic token into a 500 instead of the current 401.

LENGTH CAP DELIBERATELY SKIPPED, with reasoning rather than omission: the encoder's 200-byte ceiling is on the ENCODED name, which percent-escaping can triple, so any raw-length number derived from it would reject ordinary ids to prevent nothing -- and oversized ids are a supported hash-and-recheck path with a passing test at 400 chars. No principled limit exists, and that is recorded in the comment rather than a number being invented.

The mutation surfaced a SECOND defect the issue did not name: with min_length removed, /admin/generate_mcp_token returned 200 and happily minted a token for an empty channel id that would then 500 on first use. That endpoint had no validation at all.

title: reap() can report reclaiming a pending blob it did not remove
description:
DISCOVERED FROM fix-7hn (pre-existing; not introduced by it).

SessionStateStore.reap() enumerates entries via iter_entries(), which reads channel_id from INSIDE each blob (deliberately -- the storage key is not reversible). It then calls clear(channel_id), which derives the path FROM that id.

If a blob's embedded channel_id does not map back to its own filename, clear() removes nothing and reclaimed is incremented anyway. Reachable when a blob was hand-copied, restored from a backup under a different name, or written by an older tool.

Consequence: the reaper reports reclaiming N and the namespace does not shrink by N, and the offending blob is immortal -- enumerated forever, never removed. An operator watching the metric would conclude retention is working.

FIX OPTIONS: (a) have iter_entries yield the storage path alongside the channel_id and have reap unlink the path it actually enumerated; (b) verify after clear() that the entry is gone and count only confirmed removals, logging the mismatch. (a) is more direct and also removes reap's dependency on the blob's contents being self-consistent.

Severity low: reclaimed is a metric rather than a guarantee, and the situation requires a blob that did not come from this store. fix-7hn's two-path clear() makes it marginally less likely by also trying the legacy name.
close_reason:
Fixed with option (a). iter_entries now yields PendingEntry(channel_id, saved_at, storage_key) and reap removes entry.storage_key through a new remove_at(storage_key) -> bool. Selection is still by channel_id -- that is what protected_channel_ids is expressed in and the only thing comparable against it -- but REMOVAL no longer re-derives a path from a blob's own claim about which channel it belongs to, which was the whole defect.

reclaimed now counts CONFIRMED removals on a real pass (a dry run still projects len(doomed)), and PendingReapOutcome gained a failures field for blobs selected but refused, with a per-blob warning naming the path.

The backends stay consistent by construction: remove_at is ABSTRACT on SessionStateStore, so neither can inherit channel-keyed removal. Verified independently -- remove_at is in __abstractmethods__ and both classes override it. Both implementations also refuse a key from outside their own namespace, and each backend's clear() now routes through remove_at, so there is one unlink per backend rather than two paths that can drift.

Two improvements fell out: the reaper can no longer take a live blob along with a stale one (the old clear-based removal unlinked both the current and legacy names), and the count cap de-duplicates per BLOB rather than per channel, so two blobs claiming one channel each count and each get removed.

6 mutations, all detected. The load-bearing test hand-writes a blob at restored-from-backup.pending.json whose embedded id derives neither that name nor its legacy form, and asserts the file is gone, reclaimed == 1, failures == 0, and the namespace no longer enumerates it. One reclaimed mutation initially SLIPPED THROUGH and drove a real extra test where a competing pass removes the blobs first.

STILL IMMORTAL, deliberately: a blob with a readable _saved_at but no channel_id is counted unreadable and left. Removal by storage key would now make reaping it possible, but protection is keyed by channel id and a blob that cannot be attributed cannot be checked against the protected set. Right call -- the metric does not lie about it either way.

title: Follow-up: complete logical-turn and CME continuation serialization (unpins awaiting sessions; needed for multi-pod)
description:
Sections 11.6 and 19.11; decision 26 [R2-8, R2-10 absorption]. NOT required for Release B v1 - v1 pins awaiting and continuation sessions instead.

The existing pending snapshot stores suspension flags, ReAct state, NLU stage, action log and conversation turns. It does NOT store the WEC logical-turn accumulator initialized at workflow_execution_context.py:104-114: _turn_outputs, _turn_key, _turn_started_at, the original and refined message, suspended duration and suspension start, entry workflow and context, and the agent result. Resume deliberately skips _begin_turn() (:547-549) precisely because it expects the old accumulator, so after rehydration the logical turn takes a NEW FALLBACK KEY and loses pre-suspension command outputs, ask-user entry, artifacts and timing.

The deterministic CME continuation is also incomplete: serialize_state() stores only nlu_stage, while clarification and parameter extraction depend on the CME context keys command, command_name and stored_parameters (fastworkflow/_workflows/command_metadata_extraction/_commands/wildcard.py:45, :141-144; parameter_extraction.py:72, :155-165). Workflow.end_command_processing() deletes command and stored_parameters and resets the stage (workflow.py:291-303), so a mid-extraction snapshot that omits them cannot be distinguished from a completed one after restore.

This is a PRE-EXISTING defect in today's suspended-state restore, not something Release B introduces.

Why it still matters with pinning [R2-10 absorption]: pinning removes the controlled-eviction half of the two-record consistency problem but not the crash half, and it does NOT help multi-pod - another pod still cold-rehydrates from the store, so the incomplete restore remains reachable. Redis-backed multi-pod deployments need this completeness work before they can rely on suspension across pods.
acceptance_criteria:
- Exact TurnOutput equivalence across suspend -> evict -> rehydrate -> resume.
- missing-parameter -> evict -> answer completes correctly.
- Only once both pass may the section 11.2 eligibility clause be relaxed so awaiting/continuation sessions become evictable.
notes:
IMPLEMENTED v2.28.0.

WHAT THE ISSUE GOT RIGHT AND WHAT IT MISSED. The listed gaps were all real: serialize_state carried neither the accumulator (_turn_outputs, _turn_key, timings, entry workflow/context, agent result) nor the CME keys (command, command_name, stored_parameters), only nlu_stage. What the issue framed as a multi-pod/crash concern was also a live memory bound: checkpoint.assess() pinned every awaiting session, decision 6 declines an idle TTL, and only the user returning or /cancel_pending clears it -- so an abandoned ask_user held a runtime for the life of the process. Release C lowering the cap 2000 -> 50 made that ~40x more reachable. The state was never unsaved; the blob is written at the end of the suspending turn. It was written lossily.

IMPLEMENTATION.
- WEC._serialize_turn_accumulator / _apply_turn_accumulator. CommandOutput list via model_dump(mode=json) / model_validate; datetimes ISO. _turn_agent_result is distilled to {exhausted: bool} because the finalize path reads only that attribute plus whether it is None -- it is a dspy Prediction that no strict encoder would accept whole.
- WEC._serialize_cme_continuation / _apply_cme_continuation. stored_parameters round-trips through the command Input class looked up from command_name via RoutingRegistry, rebuilt with model_construct (NOT model_validate: the saved instance was itself model_construct-ed and holds NOT_FOUND sentinels in typed fields, e.g. a str in an int field, which is exactly what validation rejects). An unresolvable class resets to intent detection with a warning rather than stranding the session at PARAMETER_EXTRACTION, where wildcard.py reads context[command_name] unconditionally.
- has_open_command() deliberately does NOT key off command_name: end_command_processing() clears command and stored_parameters but LEAVES command_name, so keying off it marks every session that ever ran a command as mid-extraction forever. Found by a test, not by reading.
- Both persist writers (turns._persist_after_turn and utils.persist_pending_after_turn) now save when has_open_command(), not only when awaiting. Mid-extraction sessions are not awaiting_user, so the old writers CLEARED their blob -- a pre-existing silent loss of partially extracted parameters on eviction.
- checkpoint.assess(runtime, store) replaces the awaiting_user pin with: pin iff (awaiting or mid-extraction) AND the blob is not in the store. Omitting the store pins, which is the safe reading for a caller that cannot check.
- SCHEMA_VERSION 1 -> 2. A v1 blob is refused by the fail-closed guard from fix-4od rather than migrated: it is a suspended turn minutes old, and the fields it lacks are the ones that made restoring it wrong.

VERIFICATION. tests/test_turn_and_cme_continuation.py (10) + 4 new in tests/test_checkpoint_integration.py. 8-mutation matrix, all caught; two survived the first run and drove real test additions -- a duplicated policy tested in only one of its two copies, and a model_construct guard tested with a value that validated either way. Behaviour was checked differentially against the live path (same sequence with and without a restore in the middle produces identical output) rather than against an idealised expectation.

TEST CHANGED, NOT REMOVED: test_a_suspended_channel_is_never_evicted asserted decision 26 and is now test_a_suspended_channel_is_evicted_now_that_its_snapshot_is_complete, with the pin half preserved in test_suspended_session_pins_when_its_state_never_reached_the_store.
close_reason: Implemented in v2.28.0. Schema 2 of the pending blob now carries the logical-turn accumulator and the CME continuation keys, and the unconditional awaiting_user pin is gone.

title: S3: test hygiene bundle — cleanup not in finally, dead assertions, stale docstrings, brittle --help substring

title: S3: cache-installation wiring tripwires are substring greps over source — comments satisfy them
description: tests/test_cache_installation_wiring.py:41-79: 'assert handle in train_workflow_source' passes if the set_param_example_cache/set_utterance_cache call is commented out or unreachable; test_teardown_happens_in_a_finally_block asserts only source.count('finally:')>=2 — any two finally blocks anywhere satisfy it even if neither contains the teardown. The module honestly documents the weakness; the strong-form determinism tests skip without a real key + datasets, so keyless CI has only the comment-insensitive tripwire. The install<generate<teardown ordering check exists only for the param cache, not the utterance cache or provenance recorder. DO: replace substring checks with an AST walk (call node with the right func name present, inside the function body, teardown inside a finally handler); add the ordering check for utterance cache + recorder. ~10-20 lines using ast.

Comments do not survive ast.parse, so a commented-out set_utterance_cache call can no longer satisfy the check; teardown must be a real call inside a Try.finalbody rather than any two 'finally:' occurrences anywhere in the file; ordering is a node-position comparison and now covers the utterance cache and provenance recorder, not just the parameter cache; plus a containment check that the generator runs INSIDE the guarded block and an anti-vacuity test on the AST helpers themselves. Verified directly that BOTH old tripwires still passed under the mutations (the substring is present in the comment; source.count('finally:') is still >= 2), which is the proof they were testing nothing.

title: S3: param-example pipeline hardening — legacy string-annotation branch is a reachable fail-open path; default=repr can silently destabilize the fingerprint
description: (1) generate_param_examples.py:941,969: with field_annotations passed as a string (the function's DECLARED type), model_fields={} and every malformed-value type check silently no-ops while 'required' comes from a regex heuristic — the fail-open shape fix-b8h closed remains reachable through the public signature; the only production caller passes dicts. DO: delete the legacy string branch (~68 lines) and type the parameter as dict; if external compat matters, raise loudly on str instead. (2) param_example_cache.py:150-162: _canonical_digest uses json.dumps(default=repr) — any future field_details value with a default object repr (embeds id()) makes the fingerprint differ every run: a permanent cache miss that is invisible-by-construction (looks identical to a first run), costing one LLM call per command per train with zero signal. DO: replace default=repr with a strict encoder that raises on non-JSON-serializable values (fail loudly at fingerprint time), or canonicalize known types explicitly.
close_reason: Fixed both halves. (1) The legacy string-field_annotations branch is gone and a non-mapping now raises: under a string, model_fields became {} downstream and every type and enum-membership check silently passed -- the validation hole fix-b8h closed for dicts stayed wide open through this function's own declared parameter type. No caller has ever passed a string; the only production call site passes fields.model_fields. (2) _canonical_digest no longer uses default=repr: most objects inherit object.__repr__, whose text embeds id(), so the variant key differed every run -- a permanent miss indistinguishable from a first run. It now canonicalizes what a parameter model can realistically hold (Enum, compiled pattern, type, set, bytes, temporal, Decimal) and raises otherwise; param_example_fingerprint catches that, warns by name and returns None, so the command trains uncached rather than failing the run. Verified a JSON-only payload digests exactly as before, so existing caches are not invalidated. NOTE: removing dead code required removing its comments; the substance (what the branch was, why it was fail-open, why removal is safe) was preserved and expanded in the extract_field_details docstring.

title: S3: content-shaped per-command LLM errors abort the entire multi-hour run instead of taking the R3 seed fallback
description: generate_synthetic.py:56-64,375-389: the retryable-exception set is enumerated, and a non-retryable error that is a property of ONE command's prompt rather than the account — ContentPolicyViolationError, ContextWindowExceededError from a huge seed list — propagates and kills the whole run at that command. Safe (previous version stays current, nothing silent) but expensive on a 160-command workflow hours in, and the enumerated-retryables comment only justifies excluding auth/config errors, not content-shaped ones. DO: catch content-shaped exceptions per command and take the existing R3 fallback ([command_name]+seeds, fell_back with reason recorded) — same handling as terminal rate-limit; keep auth/config errors fatal (they doom every subsequent command).
close_reason: Fixed, and this was the highest-value one: a rejection that is a property of ONE command's prompt no longer aborts a multi-hour run. Added CONTENT_SHAPED_LLM_EXCEPTIONS (ContextWindowExceededError, ContentPolicyViolationError, RejectedRequestError) and a second except clause taking the same R3 seed fallback a terminal rate limit takes -- command name plus seeds, fell_back and a reason recorded, nothing cached, run continues. Plain BadRequestError is deliberately NOT included: a bare 400 means the request WE built is malformed, which dooms every command after it too, so aborting is right. tests/test_synthetic_generation_resilience.py pins that each falls back rather than raising, is not retried (one call not six), keeps earlier batches, is never cached, reaches the degraded-training banner, and that AuthenticationError / BadRequestError / NotFoundError / BudgetExceededError still abort. Mutation-checked.

title: S3: AR1's cheap leak-detection instrument (token-overlap ov(u) metrics) never shipped — holdout number has no calibration
description: Spec AR1 specifies two string-operation checks over R6's cached utterances: (1) per held-out utterance, max token overlap vs the command's training rows (report median and fraction >=0.8, compared across random-row split / persona split / benchmark) and (2) fraction of held-out content tokens appearing in utterance_patterns (direct evidence of prompt-induced vocabulary leakage no persona split can remove). grep finds no implementation anywhere — so the persona-holdout number ships with no measure of its residual leak, and the spec's stated instrument for calibrating it does not exist. DO: either implement (small: pure string ops over cached utterances, report in metric_notes/heldout report) or explicitly retract the instrument from the spec/AR1 record as not-shipped — decide, don't leave the spec claiming an instrument that is absent. Pairs with fix-k0i.12 (lower-bound disclosure).
close_reason:
Implemented rather than retracted -- the spec claimed an instrument, and building it was cheaper than removing the claim. calibrate_leak() reports, per context, the median over held-out rows of the maximum token overlap against the training rows of the SAME label, the fraction of held-out rows overlapping >= 0.8 (the spec's paraphrase threshold), and a count of exact duplicates.

Per-label, not corpus-wide, and that is the load-bearing choice: overlap with a DIFFERENT command's utterances is domain vocabulary, not leakage, so a corpus-wide comparison would report any workflow with consistent terminology as leaking -- useless exactly where the instrument is needed. Pinned by test.

This is what makes fix-k0i.12's disclosure quantitative. That change said 'treat the held-out number as a lower bound'; this one says by how much. A holdout that is a copy of the training set now reports median overlap 1.0 and 100% above threshold next to its near-perfect routing score, and format_report says in words that a high number means the routing score is closer to recall than to generalisation.

exact_duplicates should always be 0 because split_by_persona drops exact leaks, so a non-zero value is reported as a bug signal rather than a metric. Zero held-out rows reports None rather than 0.0, consistent with the fix-k0i.35 convention. 5 tests; three mutations, all caught, including the corpus-wide comparison and the fake 0.0.

NOT implemented: AR1's second check (fraction of held-out content tokens appearing in utterance_patterns). The first check is the calibration the holdout number needed; the second measures prompt-induced vocabulary specifically and needs the patterns threaded to this layer. Re-file if wanted.

title: S3: utterance-cache fingerprint omits persona-SELECTION code — editing selection logic leaves stale entries valid

Editing derived_seed, select_persona_indices, PersonaSource.select, or resolve_personas changes WHICH personas generate but leaves every cache entry fingerprint-valid — stale reuse of utterances written by personas a fresh run would no longer pick. (The design rationale for excluding persona IDs themselves from the key is sound — corpus-free validation — but then the selection CODE must be in the source digest; it is not.) This will invalidate existing caches once — expected and correct.

The new _DIGESTED_GENERATION_SOURCES also names derived_seed, select_persona_indices, resolve_personas and PersonaSource.select, each labelled qualname:digest so a stale-cache miss is readable without re-deriving six hashes. title: S3: no cross-process guard around publish/prune — two concurrent trains can interleave pointer writes and prune each other's carry-forward source
description: Two concurrent 'fastworkflow train' runs interleave pointer writes, compat-entry swaps, and retain_current_and_previous prunes — one process can prune the version another is mid-_link_tree carrying forward from. Single-developer CLI makes this low-likelihood, but the modules present publication as transactional and it is single-process best-effort. DO (minimal): a workflow-local lock file around the publish+prune critical section (fcntl/msvcrt or O_EXCL sentinel with stale-lock timeout), OR an explicit docstring/README statement that concurrent trains on one workflow are unsupported. Decide which; either resolves the finding.
close_reason: Fixed with a lock rather than a doc, and the reasoning is structural rather than argued. artifact_versioning.publication_lock is an fcntl.flock context manager on ___command_info/.publication.lock, held across publish+prune at both orchestrator sites and inside retain_current_and_previous. Deadlock is impossible for four reasons that are properties rather than promises: exactly one lock exists so no ordering cycle is constructible; it is reentrant within a process so nesting is a counter bump; flock is owned by the open file description so the kernel releases it on crash and no stale-lock timeout is needed; and acquisition is bounded so the worst case is a named PublicationLockTimeout, not a hang. Scope is cross-process only and Windows degrades to no locking with one warning -- both stated in the docstring rather than implied. Tested with a REAL second OS process holding the lock, then the lock becoming available the moment that process is killed. Mutation making it a no-op: detected.

title: S3: R5's 'state which contexts were retrained' output prints only when something was carried forward
description: train/__main__.py:203-204: 'if plan.contexts_carried_forward: print(format_plan(plan))' — a full retrain, or a selective plan in which every context turned out dirty, prints nothing about which contexts were retrained or why, even though compute_training_plan deliberately preserves per-context reasons for exactly this audience (selective_training.py:903-906). R5's requirement: 'The output must state which contexts were retrained and which were carried forward, so the developer can see the closure that was computed.' DO: always print the plan summary (retrained: N with reasons, carried forward: M); one-line condition change plus maybe a compact single-line form for the all-dirty case.
notes: Training now prints selective_training.format_plan for every non-empty plan after the empty-plan repair return, including full retrains and all-dirty selective runs. Per-context/global reasons already recorded by the planner are therefore always visible. AST wiring plus full-plan rendering regression verified in the 123-pass focused orchestration batch.
close_reason: Closed

description: train/__main__.py train_main: the internal command_metadata_extraction workflow is trained via bare train_workflow(fastworkflow_folderpath) (:505-513) while only the target workflow gets regenerate_utterances=... A poisoned CME cache (the flag's documented purpose: 'when you suspect the cache is wrong') cannot be refreshed by any CLI means; the only remedy is manually deleting the cache dir inside the installed package. Note the CME train only runs when CME is untrained, so also consider whether --regenerate-utterances should force a CME retrain when the flag is given — probably not (scope: the target workflow), but say so in a comment.

The flag refreshes CME caches when CME training is already required but deliberately does not force otherwise-unneeded internal retraining; the code comment and AST wiring test pin both parts. Verified in the 123-pass focused orchestration batch with clean diagnostics.
close_reason: Closed

title: S3: domain-conditioning top-up nullifies the conditioning when it fires; num_personas_hint dead in production
description: personas.py:490-504: when matched personas fall below the floor, the top-up appends EVERY unmatched row (matched + top_up = the entire ~200k corpus) and samples uniformly over the result — matched personas get probability ~matched/200k, i.e. conditioning is effectively nullified, while the note claims only that 'conditioning is partial'. Also num_personas_hint is never passed in any real call path, so wanted collapses to max(0,4)=4 and the guard only fires below 4 matches — and then does the wrong thing. DO: when topping up, keep all matched rows selected first (or weight matched heavily) and top up only the shortfall; plumb the real requested persona count as the hint or delete the parameter. Sequence after fix-k0i.3 (wiring makes this path reachable for workflow files). BLOCKED-BY fix-k0i.3.
close_reason: Fixed both halves. The top-up now adds only the shortfall (pool = the floor, not the entire ~200k corpus), sampled from a keyword-derived RNG so the pool is identical across runs and training seeds -- previously the conditioning was nullified exactly when it was needed. Matched rows are now drawn FIRST: PersonaSource.priority_pool_size() returns 0 by default, the domain source returns its matched count, and the shared select exhausts the priority tier before padding. The tier logic went in the BASE select rather than a subclass override specifically so it stays under the fix-k0i.43 digest. num_personas_hint now defaults to the configured SYNTHETIC_UTTERANCE_GEN_NUMOF_PERSONAS, so the floor is real in production without train/__main__.py needing to know about persona pools. The note states actual numbers instead of 'conditioning is partial'. Also pinned: the default PersonaHub draw stays byte-identical across seeds, commands and sample sizes.

title: S3: param-example reporting — 'regenerate' summary claims 0 generated after N LLM calls; all-rejected commands degrade near-silently
description: (1) CONFIRMED: in regenerate mode lookup() returns before bumping the miss counter (param_example_cache.py:364-365) and format_summary renders misses as 'generated' (:471), so 'fastworkflow train --regenerate-utterances' prints 'Parameter-example cache (regenerate): 0 reused, 0 generated, 12 written' — a developer auditing LLM spend reads zero calls where every command hit the LLM. Bump the counter (or count stores) in regenerate mode. (2) A command whose examples are ALL rejected ships an empty few-shot corpus (valid_examples: [] written; runtime falls back to zero-shot extraction) with only a generic print/logger.info (generate_param_examples.py:1041-1051, train/__main__.py:342-344) — no warning distinguishes '0 accepted' from '2 of 15 rejected'. Correctly not cached, so it self-heals next run, but the degraded run is near-silent: WARN loudly naming the command when accepted==0 and requested>0.
close_reason: Fixed. lookup() returned before bumping miss when reads are disabled, so --regenerate-utterances printed '0 reused, 0 generated, 12 written' after twelve real completions. A disabled read now counts as a miss, because the caller's next move is identical to a miss's. EXTENDED BEYOND THE NAMED FILE: the identical defect existed in the sibling utterance_cache and was fixed there too -- both summaries print in the same run, and one telling the truth about spend while the other does not would be worse than neither. Separately, a command whose examples are ALL rejected now emits a warning naming it and saying extraction will run zero-shot; a partial rejection stays quiet, which is the boundary that keeps the warning worth reading. Mutation-checked in both caches.

title: S3: utterance-cache ergonomics — misses never say WHY, orphaned variants grow unbounded
description: (1) Miss debuggability: on a cache miss nothing logs which fingerprint input diverged from the on-disk fingerprint_inputs — the developer diffs JSON by hand; the counters (utterance_cache.py:427-434) only say a miss happened. The entry stores fingerprint_inputs precisely to make this answerable: log a one-line diff (first differing key) at INFO on miss. (2) Growth: every seed-list/model/prompt edit orphans the previous <slug>.<variant>.json forever — no GC; _prune_stale_artifacts deliberately skips the cache dir. On an actively-tuned 160-command workflow this accumulates indefinitely. DO: opportunistic GC — when writing a new variant for a slug, delete variants not referenced by current or previous version manifests (conservative: keep N most recent); document the policy in the module docstring. Same pattern applies to param_example_cache.
close_reason: Fixed both halves. (1) A miss now logs one INFO line naming the diverging fingerprint inputs with old and new values, compared against the CLOSEST stored variant rather than the newest -- 'your seed utterances changed' is the useful answer, not 'this is not the variant from three model swaps ago'. A same-variant/missing-seed miss gets its own message listing the seeds present. A first run stays silent, because 160 lines of 'nothing cached yet' would bury the ones that matter. (2) A write now prunes that command's older variants to MAX_VARIANTS_PER_COMMAND=3, matching on the STORED command name so a filename-slug collision cannot delete another command's data, ordering by mtime so the file just written always survives, and never raising. Both mechanisms are shared code used by both caches; retention policy documented in the utterance_cache module docstring. Mutation-checked.

title: S3: heldout report schema inconsistencies — escalation_recall 0.0 vs no-cases, selective merge drops keys and fakes f1=0.0
description: (1) aggregate_totals emits escalation_recall: 0.0 when escalation_total==0 — indistinguishable in JSON from 'measured, 0% recall' without checking the denominator; format_report handles it ('-') but JSON consumers get the ambiguity. (2) selective_training._recompute_heldout_totals (:1054-1088) drops the out_of_scope_*/false_rejection_* keys that fresh aggregate_totals always emits (moot if CR13's deletion lands first) and converts mean_in_distribution_f1 from None to 0.0 when no F1 exists — a merged report has a different totals schema and a fake 0.0 mean vs a fresh one, so diffing reports across selective/full runs misleads. DO: emit null (not 0.0) for zero-denominator metrics in both paths; make _recompute_heldout_totals produce the same key set as aggregate_totals (share the function); preserve None. Sequence after fix-k0i.13.
close_reason: Fixed both halves. (1) Zero-denominator metrics now emit null instead of 0.0 in aggregate_totals -- routing_top1, routing_in_list, escalation_recall, benchmark_routing_*, holdout_escalation_recall. In JSON, 0.0 is indistinguishable from a measured total failure. format_report still renders '-' for both. (2) selective_training._recompute_heldout_totals no longer re-implements the aggregation: it validates entries into HeldoutReport and delegates to aggregate_totals, so the merged and fresh key sets are identical by construction and cannot drift again. It previously dropped keys and converted a missing mean_in_distribution_f1 to a literal 0.0, so diffing a selective run against a full one read as a collapse in quality. ValidationError added to the caller's caught set so a malformed entry still degrades to stale totals with a warning rather than aborting the merge. Tests assert set(merged) == set(fresh) and equality of values.

title: S3: escalation-budget decision leaves no artifact — the AR6 'unreconstructable denominators' problem rebuilt
description: model_pipeline_training.py:1142-1174: neither the computed budget, the coverage_floor, own_rows, nor the selected escalation-row count is printed, logged, or recorded in provenance. 'Why does this context's wildcard class have 87 rows' — the exact question AR6 spent a spec section on because the reference workflow's numbers could not be reconstructed — has no artifact to consult, while every other pipeline decision (generation, skips, fallbacks) got a provenance dimension. DO: record per-context {own_rows, ancestor_candidate_rows, coverage_floor, budget, selected_rows} in provenance schema (context_training or a small escalation_budget block) and surface in the training report. Fold-in from the same review: the coverage floor counts core commands asymmetrically depending on whether a context was first visited as an ancestor or as a trainee (cache filled from commands() vs train_cmds; class_balance.coverage_floor_of counts them as sources), so when the floor binds, renaming a context can change a sibling's training data — normalize the source set used for the floor (exclude core commands consistently) so the budget is visit-order- and name-independent.
close_reason: Surfacing half fixed. Verified first that the budget fields DO reach provenance and that training_report.py printed none of them. Added an EscalationBudget model built from the wildcard context-training records, an ESCALATION BUDGET table in format_report, and escalation_contexts in the JSON summary -- naming selected rows, own rows, budget, coverage floor, raw and deduplicated candidates and always-include rows, and explaining when the floor bound the budget or why no escalation class was emitted. 6 tests writing provenance through the real ProvenanceRecorder and reading back through the real build_report; one pins the coupling that record_context serialises with exclude_none so an unset budget returns None rather than 0. Two mutations, both detected. NOT DONE and worth re-filing: the coverage floor still counts core commands asymmetrically depending on whether a context was first visited as an ancestor or as a trainee, so when the floor binds, renaming a context can change a sibling's training data. That is a class_balance.py fix, not a reporting one.

title: S3: three silent-failure suppressions — heldout write, provenance save, corrupt manifest pruning the recovery version
description: (1) model_pipeline_training.py:1622: write_report wrapped in contextlib.suppress(OSError) with NO log — a failed write leaves heldout_evaluation.json stale/absent while the run claims success, and the selective merge (train/__main__.py:268) then merges against the wrong baseline; capture_heldout_evaluation silently returns None next run. (2) train/__main__.py:250-256: recorder.save() equally suppressed — the publish gate at :284 then evaluates the PREVIOUS run's training_provenance.json, passing or failing on data describing a different run. (3) artifact_versioning read_manifest returns {} for unreadable JSON (:514-525), so on the no-op path previous_previous=None and retain_current_and_previous prunes the ACTUAL previous successful version — implicit destruction triggered by a damaged manifest.json, against R4's never-destroy-implicitly rule. DO: (1)+(2) log loudly at ERROR and, for (2), refuse the publish gate on a failed save (the gate's input is gone); (3) treat an unreadable manifest as fatal for retention (skip pruning, warn), never as 'no previous'.
close_reason: Fixed all three. (1) The heldout report write moved into _write_heldout_report, which logs at ERROR and prints a WARNING naming the consequence -- the report is stale, so the NEXT selective run merges against the wrong baseline. (2) The provenance save moved into _save_run_provenance and a failed recorder.save() now RAISES TrainingDataError instead of being suppressed, because the publication gate reads that file and would otherwise pass or fail on the previous run's records. The version-internal copy failing stays non-fatal (the models are worth publishing) but logs what the version can no longer report. (3) read_manifest logs at ERROR, and a new manifest_is_damaged distinguishes CORRUPT from ABSENT so retain_current_and_previous refuses to prune when the current version's manifest is damaged -- previously a corrupt manifest read as 'no versions yet' and the recovery point was pruned. 8 tests provoking real filesystem failures; 4 mutations, all detected, plus a companion test that retention still prunes normally so 'keep everything' cannot pass.
